Before assessing or producing a translation, fix its type and vocabulary: classify it by Jakobson's intralingual, interlingual, or intersemiotic category and name the source text and language and the target text and language, since interlingual translation is the field's prototypical focus.

Treat translation as a prototype category with a periphery (adaptation, version, transcreation, localization), and when there is no single stable source text (multilingual versions, unstable, continually updated, or orally transmitted sources) broaden the source-to-target model rather than forcing the traditional configuration.

Decide whether a translation is overt (its source is tied to its culture and time, so it cannot pretend to be an original and seeks second-level functional equivalence at the level of language, register, and genre, letting target receivers eavesdrop) or covert (its source is not culture-bound, so it should read as an original through a cultural filter that adapts cultural elements at the levels of language and register), treat the distinction as a cline, and produce a version rather than a translation when the source genre has no equivalent target form.
Do not assume that close lexical fidelity to the source is a universal goal; some traditions and text purposes legitimately expect a substantial change of form.
Keep the distinction between strategy (the overall orientation of the translated text) and procedure (a specific technique used at a given point) straight when analysing or prescribing a translation.

Locate any translation task or study on the discipline map before proceeding: distinguish pure research (theoretical, and descriptive along product, function, and process orientations) from applied work (training, aids, criticism, policy), and note which partial-theory restrictions (medium, area, rank, text-type, time, problem) apply, since several may apply at once.
Choose the translation theory and method by the goals of the task, not by allegiance to a school, and prefer describing what translation actually does over prescribing what it should do.
Treat interpreting as a parallel sub-discipline with its own requirements rather than as a sub-type of written translation.
Ensure specialized translation training and competence include instruction in the subject domains to be translated (such as law, medicine, finance, or science).

Default to sense-for-sense translation rather than slavish word-for-word rendering, which produces absurd and opaque target text, but treat sacred or otherwise sensitive texts as an exception warranting closer attention to the words, syntax, and ideas, and match the degree of stylistic polishing to the source rather than embellishing a plain source text.

Expect the recurring cross-cultural swing between literal and free translation and the systematic losses that rendering into another language incurs (reversed word order, stylistic elevation, omitted repetition, reduced paratext, restructuring), and recognize that a highly literal method that borrows everything tends to fail.

Work the Vinay and Darbelnet procedure ladder: within direct translation use borrowing, calque, or literal translation, prescribing literal rendering as the basis of good translation and sacrificing literalness only for structural or metalinguistic reasons after checking that meaning is preserved, and when a literal rendering is unacceptable on grammatical, syntactic, or pragmatic grounds move to oblique translation through transposition (change of part of speech, the commonest structural change), modulation (change of viewpoint, the touchstone of a good translator, used when a correct rendering is unidiomatic or awkward), equivalence (idiomatic rendering for idioms and proverbs), or adaptation (change of cultural reference when the source situation is absent).

Flag cases that need special care, namely directing the message to a new audience, handling sacred or highly authoritative source words, or working from an accreted or variant source, and manage the source-text instability they create.

Use Dryden's triad as a diagnostic scale, placing a rendering on the metaphrase (literal), paraphrase (sense-for-sense), or imitation (adaptation) continuum, and default to paraphrase, which keeps the author in view, over servile metaphrase or free imitation.

When no other guidance is given, follow the classic ranked prescriptions for good translation: understand the sense fully, know both languages well, avoid word-for-word and unusual or Latinate forms, and produce a natural, eloquent target form that gives a complete transcript of the ideas in the same style with the ease of the original.

When you cannot satisfy every criterion, resolve trade-offs by a fixed priority: sacrifice ease of composition before style, and style before sense or meaning, so that correspondence in meaning takes priority over correspondence in style.

Define a good translation by its effect on the target reader, so completely transfusing the merit of the original that a target reader apprehends and feels it as a source reader does, and pitch it to the target readership's level of education and understanding, which usually differs from the translator's own.

Treat translation as inferential communication, making the target optimally relevant so the receiver derives adequate contextual effects without unnecessary effort by supplying communicative clues, and decide whether and how to communicate the informative intention, whether to translate descriptively or interpretively, and the degree of resemblance to the source from the receiver's cognitive environment, since a translation can fail when it does not match the audience's expectations for form or prestige.

Treat translation as a distinct linguistic genre with its own norms and ends whose value lies in forcing the reader out of native linguistic habits and into the foreign author's world; correspondingly, a translation that reduces the work to transmissible information conveys only the inessential and is, on this view, bad translation.

Treat translation as at once interpretation and creation, involving a choice among the source's possible interpretations and a choice among the target's possible expressions of that meaning, and expect the translator in practice to apply a pessimistic minimax strategy — accepting the solution promising the most effect for the least effort provided its value clears the minimum his standards admit — while recognizing that the importance he assigns a stylistic device is a relative value weighed against competing values such as linguistic purity, that preserving a device is an implicit bet on what fraction of readers will feel the language violated, and that a preserved formal feature communicates only to the subset of readers competent to decode it (Sapphic metre versus apparent free verse), so the likely audience composition must be weighed.

Orient every translation consciously on the domestication-to-foreignization axis, choosing between moving the writer toward the reader (naturalizing) and moving the reader toward the writer (foreignizing), and know which pole you are choosing and why.

Orient a translation on the domestication-foreignization axis, where domestication is an ethnocentric, fluent, invisible reduction of the foreign to receiving values that moves the author toward the reader and dominates Anglo-American culture, and foreignization chooses a foreign text and a non-fluent, estranging method that makes the translator visible and highlights the source's identity by moving the reader toward the author, realizing foreignization through text choice and techniques such as close adherence to structure, calques, archaisms, and heterogeneous discourse, and treating the two as a continuum on an ethical level of values and a discursive level of fluency versus resistancy while noting that foreignization is relative and historically contingent.

Assess and produce translations against explicit, operational criteria rather than the vague vocabulary of early theory, using rubrics that cover accuracy (correct information transfer and full comprehension), appropriate vocabulary, idiom, terminology and register, cohesion, coherence and organization, and technical accuracy.

Read literal in its modern sense as close lexical translation, a defect only at the extreme that breaks target naturalness (false friends or imported unnatural syntax), and by default aim for a natural target text that reads as if originally written in the target language unless a foreignizing effect is intended.

Condition the method on text type and audience, seeking the same impression on the target reader as the original produced and balancing between sounding like a translation and being aggressively idiosyncratic: make readable renderings for informative periodical prose but very close renderings for politically sensitive texts, and allow for non-native target readers.
Mine translators' prefaces and self-accounts as evidence of the translation method and stance adopted, while allowing for their bias.

Weigh translators' self-accounts as evidence of method and stance while allowing for bias and their intuitive voice-led vocabulary, recognizing that much of the labour behind a translation is invisible and that a translation is a non-neutral critical act whose ideology resides in the translator's voicing, stance, and place of enunciation.

Treat cross-language equivalence as partial and relative rather than identity: because there is no full equivalence between code-units, translate whole messages rather than code-units, and treat translatability as a matter of degree and adequacy, since all cognitive content is conveyable in some form.

Take the message, not the code-unit, as the unit of equivalence: since synonymy is ordinarily not complete equivalence and there is usually no full equivalence between code-units across languages, translation recodes two equivalent messages in two different codes ('equivalence in difference', the cardinal problem of language), which is why comparing languages by their mutual translatability and building differential bilingual dictionaries (intension and extension) and grammars is of high theoretical and practical value.

Reject cross-code identity as the basis of translation: the referential argument fails because a word signifies through its systematic relations within its code, not through the object, the conceptual argument fails for lack of any grammar-cognition correlation, and the universals argument yields only trivial universals; point-by-point identity would turn translation into copying, mimicry, or transliteration because it cannot capture the surrounding code structure (a sentential adverb acceptable in Spanish is despised in written English), and identity is useless because universal grammar is a matter of absolute competence whereas translation is a matter of probabilistic performance — its very interest springing from the structural mismatch of codes, so that where whole structures are identical the recoding is academic and not even worthy of the name translation.

Resolve the categories the source and target languages obligatorily force (gender, aspect, kinship fields), since languages differ chiefly in what they must convey rather than what they may, do not treat a lexical gap as untranslatable, and reserve the untranslatable verdict for poetry where form and sound are inseparable from sense and creative transposition is required.

Treat meaning as contextual and functional, since a word acquires meaning in context and produces culture-varying responses, and distinguish linguistic, referential, and emotive or connotative meaning when analysing it.

Use Nida's analytical procedure and semantic tools where helpful: analyse the source into basic kernel elements, transfer them, and restructure into the target, and use componential and semantic-structure analysis to discriminate the senses of related words, especially between widely differing languages.

Choose the equivalence orientation by purpose: use formal equivalence, which matches source form and content closely as in gloss translations, for academic or legal texts that give the reader access to the source language and customs, and use dynamic or functional equivalence, the closest natural equivalent tailored to the receptor with adjustments of grammar, lexicon, and cultural references and no source interference, elsewhere, noting that dynamic equivalence minimizes source foreignness in a way culturally oriented theorists criticize.

Check a translation against Nida's four requirements (it makes sense, conveys the spirit and manner of the original, has a natural and easy form, and produces a similar response) while treating equivalent effect as a graded, unverifiable goal that cannot be objectively measured across different cultures and times.

Guard against overtranslation when pursuing the closest natural equivalent, such as choosing target equivalents that share an unintended feature and create a spurious link, and take Nida's central lesson to be centring the receptor and their cultural expectations rather than seeking strict word-for-word equivalence.

Because equivalent effect can be illusory when a text is out of target space and time, follow Newmark in choosing method by text type: use semantic translation, which renders the exact contextual meaning as closely as target syntax allows, respects context, interprets, stays within the source culture, and tends to overtranslate, for serious literature and authoritative, political, or expressive texts, and use communicative translation, which produces an effect on its readers close to the original's, is smoother and target-culture oriented, and tends to undertranslate, for the majority of texts such as non-literary, technical, informative, and publicity writing, keeping semantic translation distinct from mere literal rendering of source lexis and syntax.

Keep a literal word-for-word rendering wherever it secures equivalent effect, since it is then the most economical valid choice, but switch to communicative translation when a literal or semantic rendering would be abnormal or would not secure equivalent effect, and allocate cognitive effort to the hard problems while spending less where a literal procedure already yields a reasonable result.

Distinguish Koller's correspondence (system-level contrast, the source of false friends and interference) from equivalence (relations in specific source-target pairs), treat competence in equivalences rather than correspondences as the mark of translation competence, and actively watch for false friends and lexical, morphological, and syntactic interference.

Escalate through Koller's five equivalence relations by the needs of the communicative situation, trying denotative (content), then connotative (near-synonym and style), text-normative (text-type norms), pragmatic or communicative (receiver-oriented), and formal or expressive (form, wordplay, style), and weigh connotative equivalence carefully, since it is the hardest and only approximate and involves dimensions of formality, social usage, geographical origin, stylistic effect, frequency, register range, evaluation, and emotion.

When comparing source and target, use an explicit invariant (tertium comparationis) whose appropriateness depends on circumstances, audience, and the equivalence type sought, and remember that equivalence is always relative and its definition circular, so any judgement is inevitably partly subjective.

For legal documents and equally valid multilingual treaties use a technique close to formal equivalence with little room for adjustment, yet ensure each version still produces the same response, because small grammatical divergences between versions can shift meaning and create legal confusion, loopholes, or interpretive discrepancy.
Apply an analytical model prospectively to a source text that is about to be translated rather than only retrospectively to existing translations.

Use the supplementary procedures and watch their hazards, weighing amplification against economy in word count, catching false friends that deceive, explicitating implicit information, and generalizing to a more general term, and above all, since translation inevitably loses some source nuance, compensate by introducing a gain at the same or another point in the text.

Separate obligatory from optional shifts, since servitude covers transpositions and modulations forced by the language systems while option covers non-obligatory choices of style and emphasis, and make option, the realm of stylistics, the translator's main concern by choosing among the available options to express the message's nuances.

Follow an explicit procedure from source to target: identify the units of translation (the smallest segment whose signs should not be translated individually, not the single word), evaluate their content, reconstruct the metalinguistic context, evaluate the stylistic effects, and produce and revise the target text.

Analyse translation shifts against a system-level baseline, treating a shift as a departure from formal correspondence, of level (grammar in one language, lexis in another) or category (structural, class, unit or rank, or intra-system), and judge equivalence by communicative features such as function, relevance, situation, and culture rather than by formal criteria alone or by idealized invented examples divorced from whole texts.

Analyze departures from formal correspondence as Catford's shifts, of two major types: level shifts, which render a source item at one linguistic level by a target equivalent at another and are possible only between grammar and lexis (Russian perfective aspect, having no marked English counterpart, is rendered lexically by a word such as 'achieve'), and category shifts, which presuppose some formal correspondence and come in four kinds — structure shifts (the most frequent), class shifts, unit or rank shifts, and intra-system shifts — noting that normal unbounded translation sets equivalences at whatever rank fits while rank-bound translation confined below the sentence produces bad translation, and that an intra-system shift (English 'advice' becoming French plural 'des conseils') shows even corresponding systems do not guarantee term-for-term equivalence.

Preserve source markedness in the target text when it carries a communicative function, since a marked source item usually needs a similarly marked rendering but not always and the translator should find the reason behind the markedness, and recognize the translator's own discursive presence, since translational stylistics can recover the translator's style and intentions from the target choices.

Treat translation as an interpretive cognitive process: read and understand to grasp the sense and authorial intention including implicit meaning, work from the deverbalized sense to avoid transcoding and calques, re-express, and verify, remembering that translators are privileged readers who do not feel equally close to all texts.

Investigate the translation process with think-aloud protocols triangulated with video observation, interviews and questionnaires, keystroke logging, and eye-tracking, but treat the findings cautiously, since think-aloud may capture only a reported intermediate stage, verbalizing slows and alters segmentation, automatic processes are missed, and designs still need replication and standardization.

When applying a shift taxonomy to real text, expect the recurring problem of fixing segmentation boundaries, and remember that such taxonomies describe the translation product rather than the process, with fuzzy category boundaries and little account of the effect on the reader.

Work at the level of the whole text and map its predominant function to a method: an informative text is content-focused and its target should transmit referential content in plain prose with explicitation as needed; an expressive text is form-focused and its target should transmit aesthetic form by an identifying method adopting the author's perspective; an operative text is appeal-focused and its target should elicit the desired response by an adaptive method aiming at equivalent effect; and an audio-medial or multimodal text adds a supplementary method with image and sound, judging the target by transmission of the source's predominant function.

Assess a target text against Reiss's adequacy criteria (semantic, lexical, and grammatical or stylistic equivalence, and the non-linguistic determinants of situation, subject field, time, place and culture, receiver, sender, and affective implications), weighting them by text type so that semantic equivalence is prioritized for content-focused texts and metaphor is preserved more in expressive than in informative texts.

Recognize that most texts are hybrids carrying several coexisting functions, that the target function may legitimately differ from the source function, and that the method depends on far more than text type, since the translator's role and purpose and sociocultural pressures also shape the strategy, and add a phatic function for contact-maintaining language such as greetings.

Apply text-type methods with care, since they are hard to apply and may not be reversible: even the plain-prose method for informative texts fails for metaphor-rich genres like business and financial writing, whose target must use the genre's conventional lexical and conceptual metaphors or lose the expressive function.

Treat text types as prototypes on a continuum without rigid divisions, incorporating the relevant non-linguistic disciplines, but remember that an all-encompassing continuum does not by itself yield more useful results and that commercial and literary translators need differentiated training, and treat digital genres as hybrid multimodal types produced through localization.

Treat translation as purpose-driven human interaction that guides cooperation across cultural barriers (translatorial action), map its roles of initiator, commissioner, source-text producer, target-text producer, target-text user, and target-text receiver, and guide the target text's form and genre by what is functionally suitable in the target culture as the expert determines rather than by copying the source profile.
Clarify a technical term for a non-expert receiver and translate a single term consistently throughout to maintain cohesion for the target reader.

Let the purpose or skopos determine the translation, since the target must be fit for purpose and functionally adequate, so establish why the source is being translated and what the target's function will be before deciding strategy.

Apply the skopos rules in hierarchical order, ensuring first that the target fulfils its purpose, then that it is internally coherent and interpretable as coherent with the receiver's situation, knowledge, and needs, and only then that it is coherent with the source, since intertextual source-target coherence is subordinate to intratextual target coherence, which is subordinate to the skopos.

Apply functionality plus loyalty, treating functionality as the most important criterion but not a licence for anything, so that a bilateral loyalty to the source and target sides keeps the target purpose compatible with the author's intentions, limits the justifiable target functions, and requires negotiating the assignment with the client.

Translate the same source differently according to the target purpose and commission, consciously and consistently by a principle decided for each case, and state the skopos explicitly or implicitly in a commission or brief comprising a goal and its conditions such as deadline and fee, negotiated with the commissioner and with the translator advising on feasibility, letting adequacy override equivalence as the measure.

Make the translation commission an explicit instruction stating both the goal and the conditions for attaining it (including deadline and fee), negotiated with the client — who may hold an imprecise or false picture of how the text will be received, so the translator should offer argued suggestions — while remembering that a commission's realizability depends on the target culture's circumstances, not the source's (too great a discrepancy yields not a translation but at most a rewrite); this relativizes the once-dominant demand to translate 'as literally as possible' into just one legitimate skopos among many, does not require adaptation to target expectations (a deliberately marked translation and every hybrid are equally accommodated), and yields a threefold value: making an often-denied aim explicit, expanding strategy and releasing the translator from enforced literalness, and enlarging the translator's accountability to make the goal actually attained.

Do not let a fulfilled skopos excuse micro-level neglect, since a translation may be functionally adequate yet inadequate at the stylistic or semantic level of individual segments, and choose between documentary translation (a document of source-culture communication that the reader knows is a translation, including literal and exoticizing translation) and instrumental translation (an independent target-culture instrument read as an original, function-preserving where possible).

Drive a translation from the brief and source analysis: use the commission (specifying, for both source and target, the intended functions, addressees, time and place of reception, medium, and motive) to see where the two profiles diverge and to prioritize content, then analyse the source to decide feasibility, the most relevant items, and the strategy, using intratextual factors such as subject matter, content, presuppositions, text composition, non-verbal elements, lexis, sentence structure, and suprasegmental features, and apply the same pragmatic model to both source and brief so the results are comparable.

Work the functional hierarchy top-down with the intended target function paramount: compare source and target functions to choose documentary or instrumental translation, analyse the commission to decide which functional elements to reproduce and which to adapt, let the translation type set the style (documentary more source-oriented, instrumental more target-oriented), and only then tackle the lower-level linguistic problems.

Adjust for the audience and medium: omit source redundancies the target audience already knows and make explicit source meanings it would miss, respect that genre conventions vary interlingually and may be deliberately overridden to preserve a function, rename, substitute, or adapt culture-specific items absent from the target culture so the target stays functionally adequate, and respect physical and format constraints such as fixed images and caption-length limits.

Use the Hallidayan model to relate lexicogrammatical choices to a text's function in its sociocultural framework, analysing register as field, tenor, and mode mapped to the ideational, interpersonal, and textual metafunctions, and reading patterns of transitivity, modality, thematic structure, and cohesion to see how meaning is constructed and how a shift such as active to passive or a nominalization can change who is represented as responsible.

Assess translation quality by comparing the source and target register profiles (field, tenor, mode) and their genre and function, producing a statement of mismatches classified as covertly erroneous errors (dimensional mismatches in register or genre) or overtly erroneous errors (denotative mismatches or target-system errors).
Watch that register and genre shifts can soften an author's critical stance and even shift the genre, sometimes under publisher pressure for political or marketing reasons.

Analyse equivalence at multiple levels (word, above word, grammar, thematic structure, cohesion, and pragmatics) and preserve genre-appropriate thematic and information structure in the target rather than calquing source word order, which is realized differently across languages and can read as monotonous or clumsy, while remaining aware of the relative markedness of these structures.

Treat cohesion (Halliday and Hasan's five types of reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, and lexical cohesion) as language-specific, rebuilding the web of cohesive ties in the target rather than copying it and keeping the target coherent, noting that translators tend to explicitate cohesive ties, which can cause functional shifts, and that a gender- or subject-inflected target may force disambiguation of a deliberately ambiguous source, which should be chosen with awareness of the loss.

Manage pragmatic meaning across cultures by making an implicit link explicit for readers who lack the background (since coherence depends on the receiver's world knowledge), handling presupposition by making a presupposed reference explicit when target receivers lack the source receivers' background, and treating implicature through Grice's maxims of quantity, quality, relevance, and manner plus politeness, remembering that cultures operate with different cooperative maxims.

Watch how discourse-level choices shift meaning, since transitivity shifts change the ideational function and modality shifts change truth value, a translator's lexical choices can impose an ideology or discourse, idiolect and dialect carry a semiotic function hard to replicate that target literary norms may constrain, and the interpersonal function of hedges, evaluative and attitudinal language, and pronoun choice is a sensitive site where downplaying or shifting evaluation reveals the translator's interpretation.

Link strategy to a text's stable versus dynamic elements, since more stable source texts may permit a fairly literal approach while more dynamic source texts pose greater challenges where literal translation may no longer be an option.

Use discourse and register analysis as a flexible toolkit rather than a rigid one-to-one model, and heed its cautions: a source-target mismatch may be a legitimate strategy such as explicitation or compensation rather than an error, the frameworks are English-oriented and should not be imposed uncritically on other or non-European languages, and fluency-oriented linguistic approaches and Grice's maxims are culturally biased toward domestication and suit closely defined fields like technical or legal texts.

Treat subtitling as an overt, vulnerable translation constrained by on-screen space, legibility, and timing that force shortening, and expect it to normalize informal sociolect by increasing cohesion and using conventional grammar and to lose tenor markers such as a reported-speech subjunctive, which should be compensated elsewhere, while remembering that tone may be carried by the soundtrack so text-based analysis alone may miss it.
Use House's quality-assessment model chiefly to uncover errors in a formal written target text, and investigate the specific translation commission to explain the reasons behind any reworking.

Read translated literature as a system within the target culture's social, literary, and historical systems, whose position is not fixed but shifts in a dynamic hierarchy between primary (innovatory, shaping the centre) and secondary (peripheral, conservative, and the normal position), occupying a primary position when a literature is young, peripheral or weak, or in crisis or vacuum.

Adopt a descriptive, target-organized, functional, and systemic view of literary translation with continual interplay between theoretical models and case studies, focused on the norms and constraints that govern the production and reception of translations.

Analyse translation as rewriting that projects an author's image beyond its culture, controlled by professionals inside the literary system who set the dominant poetics and by patronage outside it that sets the ideology through ideological, economic, and status components, and expect that when linguistic considerations conflict with ideological or poetological ones the latter win, so ideology and the dominant target poetics dictate the strategy.

Treat translated literature as a system with its own repertoire, not a random set of texts (its works correlate in how their source texts are selected — selection always tied to the target literature's home co-systems — and in the norms they adopt), and hold its position within the literary polysystem to be variable rather than fixed: central or peripheral, innovatory (primary) or conservatory (secondary), depending on the constellation under study.

Expect translated literature to assume a central, innovating position under three conditions (one law) — when a literature is young and being established, when it is peripheral or weak within a larger group, and at turning points, crises, or vacuums — where it introduces new models and blurs the line between original and translated writing; and expect it in the peripheral position to employ secondary models and become a major factor of conservatism, adhering to norms the centre has rejected, so that a vehicle for new ideas can ossify into a systeme d'antan (empirically the 'normal' position tends to be peripheral, and rigid systems keep it extremely so).

Locate translation within the literary system's two controls: patronage, the regulatory body with ideological, economic, and status components (usually exerted through critics, and either undifferentiated under one ideology or differentiated among competing ideologies), and poetics, the code with an inventory component (genres, symbols, characters, prototypical situations) and a functional component (how literature may function in society) that is singular under undifferentiated patronage but plural and stratified into 'high' and 'low' under differentiated patronage.

Let the position of translated literature condition the strategy: when it is primary, break target conventions and produce an adequate target text that reproduces the source's textual relations, and when it is secondary, use existing target-culture models and produce more acceptable, non-adequate translations.

Do descriptive translation studies with an explicit, systematic method so findings are intersubjectively testable, comparable, and replicable, treating translations first as facts of the target culture whose position determines strategy, and applying Toury's three-phase methodology of situating the text in the target system, analysing coupled source-target pairs to identify obligatory and non-obligatory shifts, and generalizing about the patterns to reconstruct the process, repeating across similar pairs.

Treat equivalence and adequacy as non-prescriptive concepts that vary with the social, historical, and cultural situation of the text, while noting polysystem theory's tendencies to over-generalize to universal laws, to rely on a Formalist model, to favour the abstract over real-life constraints, and to be restricted to literature.

Recognize that coupled-pair mapping is ad hoc, partial, and not fully objective or replicable, so support it with an explicit repertory-of-features checklist, and do not let a target-text-only stance overlook ideological and political factors such as the source's status in its own culture, the source culture's promotion of its own literature, and the effects a translation exerts back on the source system.

Reconstruct the norms operating in a translation, which are the community's shared values turned into performance instructions, specific to a culture and time and sitting on a potency cline between rules and idiosyncrasies and graded in intensity, from the regularities in the texts and from explicit statements treated cautiously as possibly biased.

Treat being a translator as playing a socially allotted role whose prerequisite is acquiring the norms for what is suitable and for manoeuvring among competing constraints (not reducible to generating 'translation' utterances): those constraints lie on a scale between relatively absolute rules and purely individual idiosyncrasies, with the vast intersubjective middle occupied by norms (themselves a graded continuum that shift over time as whims become norms and norms harden into rules); norms translate a community's shared values into performance instructions specifying what is prescribed, forbidden, tolerated, and permitted, so — since there is no necessary identity between a norm and any verbal formulation of it, and stated norms are slanted by a desire to control — reconstruct the actual norms from regularities of behaviour rather than from what practitioners say they do.

Map the norms operating at each stage: the initial norm, the general choice between source norms giving an adequate translation and target-culture norms giving an acceptable one on a continuum; the preliminary norms of translation policy for text selection and directness of translation through an intermediate language; and the operational norms comprising matricial norms of completeness (omissions, relocations, segmentation, added passages or footnotes) and textual-linguistic norms of lexical and stylistic selection.

Use Toury's structure of translational norms: preliminary norms (with logical and chronological precedence) govern translation policy — the non-random set of factors determining which text-types and texts a culture imports at a given time — and directness, the tolerance for indirect translation through a mediating language (permitted, prohibited, tolerated, or preferred, and whether the mediation is marked, ignored, camouflaged, or denied); operational norms govern the act itself, subdividing into matricial norms (the existence, fullness, location, and segmentation of the target material, hence omissions, additions, and relocations) and textual-linguistic norms (the selection of the linguistic material).

Treat translation equivalence descriptively as a functional-relational concept, assuming equivalence between target and source and studying how it was realized and what constrained the translator rather than judging prescriptively whether the target is equivalent, in the descriptive turn that abandoned one-to-one correspondence and destabilized the notion of an original with a fixed identity.

Expect Toury's probabilistic laws when reviewing translations: the law of growing standardization modifies source textual relations toward habitual target options and loses stylistic variation, especially in a weak position, and the law of interference copies source lexical and syntactic patterning by default, whether negative or positive, and is tolerated more when translating from a prestigious source into a minor target, while the frequent use of conjoint phrases may be a universal of translation into young or weak systems.

Use Chesterman's S-universals (differences between translations and their sources, such as target texts being longer, dialect normalized, explicitation common, repetition reduced, and retranslation closer to the source) and T-universals (features of translated versus original language, such as lexical simplification, atypical patterns, and under-representation of target-specific items, found via large corpora), remembering that laws admit exceptions explainable by other laws and that the standardization and interference laws are reconciled by the social conditions of risk and reward, since translators avoid risk by standardizing or channelling interference unless rewarded otherwise.

Apply Chesterman's norms alongside Toury's: product or expectancy norms are set by readers' expectations of a translation of a given type, governed by the target tradition, genre discourse conventions, and economic and ideological factors, allow evaluative judgements, and may be validated by a norm-authority, while professional norms subordinate to them are the accountability norm of ethical responsibility to commissioner and reader, the communication norm of the translator as expert ensuring maximum communication, and the relation norm judging the appropriate source-target relation by text type, the commissioner's wishes, the author's intentions, and the readers' needs.

Describe a translation systematically at Lambert and van Gorp's four levels of preliminary data, macro-level, micro-level shifts, and systemic context, and, since a single study is legitimate but must not ignore its connections to other translations, triangulate by comparing two translations of the same source rather than concluding from one isolated study.

Note that proper names and culturally bound items are handled by opposite norms, a source-oriented strategy retaining them at the cost of pronunciation or lost allusion and a target-oriented strategy recreating sound, wordplay, and allusion, and because names may be the most culturally bound items do not generalize the overall strategy from them but use a checklist of varied features.

Recognize that euphemistic or altered translations reveal a society's dominant ideology and, for readers who cannot read the source, become the text, and that rewriting before or during translation by omitting, softening, or altering sensitive passages is driven by ideological and commercial pressures.

Read theorists' own agendas critically and detect ideological manipulation in the target text, whether from the translator or from commissioner, editor, or institutional pressure and especially in news translation, using discourse, critical-discourse, and narrative analysis, while recognizing the macro forces of censorship, the epistemicide of English academic hegemony, and language imbalance, including informal translation in multilingual cities.

Read a translation's cuts and adaptations against its imagined audience and market, which systematically shape what is suppressed, and against the distance between the source and target audiences, which forces adaptation; and judge a translator not for cutting content but for concealing it — transparency about what is cut matters more than whether something is cut.

Locate the deep problem of translating a foreign work not in the dictionary or semantic equivalence but in a compromise between two poetics in which the receiving system's poetics dominates (translators of Brecht made explicit what he wanted the audience to piece together, added italics and stage directions, and padded songs into the Broadway-musical register), against which refractors of an alien poetics deploy four strategies — accepting the works while dismissing the poetics, psychologizing the poetics as rationalized temperament, assimilating it by translating its concepts into the old terminology, or explaining it and showing the system can accommodate it; therefore do not judge translations in isolation as simply good or bad, since a later source-faithful version can afford its fidelity only because earlier compromising translations first established a bridgehead and started the critical debate, expect no necessary progression toward a single definitive translation (language, politics, and the refracting spectrum keep shifting, and literary systems are stochastic), and account for the many changes explicable only by ideology rather than comprehension — playing down or omitting charged content, raising loaded words to a nobler register, and removing profanity to satisfy the receiving system's codes.

Do not translate from a position of monolingual superiority: the native's withholding (Friday's erased rebus in Coetzee's Foe, the transmission marked 'not a story to pass on' in Morrison's Beloved) figures the limit of translation, so untranslatability can be a marked and honored condition rather than a failure to be overcome by the confident accessibility of the powerful; the too-easy accessibility of translation as a transfer of substance reduces its object, so attend instead to the rhetoric that points to the limits of translation in a marginalized speaker's use of the dominant language, remembering that reading is itself a form of translation in which the post-colonial reader-as-translator reads a dominant text critically — using what is useful, discriminating on the terrain of the original, and noticing where the text swerves or keeps its argument domestic.

Understand committed and identity-based translation: feminist theory critiques the sexist metaphors of the field and directs fidelity to the shared writing project, a committed project openly manipulates the text as a political activity with visible strategies, and identity markers such as those of queer or camp discourse may disappear, be made pejorative, or be intensified according to target-culture attitudes and commercial pressures.

Explain a translation's minimization or amplification of a marked identity-discourse by the target culture's prevailing conception of human subjectivity: French Enlightenment universalism, suspicious of subcultural identity labels and of 'the temptation of the community', leads a French translator to suppress camp where Anglo-American identity politics would foreground it — so whether a marked discourse can accrue positive value in translation depends on the target polysystem's categories (where the identity category and an established minority literature are disabled, the associated register stays marginalized), and source categories such as French 'pederastic literature' must not be conflated with the target's understanding of 'gay literature'.

Attend to power in cross-cultural translation, since translation has been active in colonization and in disseminating an image of the colonized: avoid the homogenizing translatese that flattens less powerful literatures, translate instead from an intimate understanding of the source and, where warranted, use interventionist practice that resists assimilation, and treat the translator as a non-neutral agent working in the third space.

Beware that translating a regional or social dialect with another culture's sociolect uproots the characters and superimposes the hegemonic sociolect, and that culturally loaded kinship and endearment terms handled inconsistently can disrupt a central theme of the source culture.

Contest value-free descriptions and account for the value-driven institutional network of a translation, including the publishers and editors who choose, commission, pay, and dictate method plus agents, marketing, and reviewers, and recognize the translator's invisibility in Anglo-American cultures produced both by fluent translation that creates an illusion of transparency and by readers judging a translation acceptable only when it reads as the original rather than a translation.

Investigate domesticating and foreignizing practices and the translator's invisibility by comparing source and target for tell-tale signs, interviewing translators and publishers, and examining translation volumes, trends, contracts, packaging visibility, and reviews, and take Berman's ethical aim of receiving the Foreign as Foreign, treating translation as a trial both for the target culture experiencing the foreign and for the uprooted source.

Screen a literary translation for Berman's twelve deforming tendencies (rationalization, clarification, expansion, ennoblement, qualitative and quantitative impoverishment, destruction of rhythms, of underlying networks of signification, of linguistic patternings, and of vernacular networks or their exoticization, destruction of expressions and idioms, and effacement of the superimposition of languages), refusing to replace a source idiom with a target equivalent or to seek a target vernacular for a source vernacular, and pursue instead a positive labour on the letter that attends to the work's signifying process.

Use Berman's twelve deforming tendencies as a systematic diagnostic that bears on all translating in the western tradition: rationalization, clarification, expansion, ennoblement and popularization, qualitative impoverishment, quantitative impoverishment, the destruction of rhythms, the destruction of underlying networks of signification, the destruction of linguistic patternings, the destruction of vernacular networks or their exoticization, the destruction of expressions and idioms, and the effacement of the superimposition of languages.

Analyse translation sociologically with Bourdieu's field, habitus, and capital and with the structure of international cultural exchange, its political and economic constraints, and its intermediation agents, recognizing that the translator's position is weak, poorly structured, low-paid, contract-to-contract, and often uncredited, that editors and copy-editors shape the product toward domestication, and that publishers wield the decisive power over whether a work is translated at all, an imbalance Venuti reads as cultural hegemony.

Study a translation's reception through reviews and paratexts, distinguishing peritexts (in the same volume, from author or publisher) from epitexts (freely circulating reviews, marketing, and criticism) that guide the reading, analysing reviews synchronically or diachronically against the readers' horizon of expectation, and expecting reviews to prefer fluent translations, rarely discuss the translation, and treat the translator's words as the author's own, confirming the translator's invisibility.

Critique a translation by analyzing its concrete textual features — lexicon, syntax, prosody, discourse — and explaining them through the translator's literary habits, the traditions of the translating language, and the cultural values and political interests those choices invest in, rather than by an abstract fidelity score.

Treat literary translation as an interpretive act proceeding through Steiner's hermeneutic motion of initiative trust, aggression, incorporation, and compensation, grounding faithfulness ethically in restoring the balance that appropriation disrupts, and recognizing that incorporation can enrich or infect the target culture and enhance or consume the translator and that great translation arises from an unresolved but expressive tension between resistant difference and elective affinity that is greater the closer the two cultures are.

Keep the ethics of the foreign in view: translating is at once sympathetic and violent, exploitive and ethically restorative (Steiner), so great translation must carry the most precise possible sense of the resistant — the barriers intact at the heart of understanding — rather than erase the text's difficulty, and beware that the maxim that a translation should not seem translated mystifies its own appropriation (Meschonnic), masking an annexation of the foreign under an illusion of transparency that, forgetting its history, risks imperialism.

Model translation as Steiner's fourfold hermeneutic motion — initiative trust, aggression, incorporation, and restitution — which supersedes the sterile triad of literalism, paraphrase, and free imitation and is inherent in even the rudiments of translation; its first move, trust, is an a priori leap that grants 'there is something there' to understand and that the transfer will not be void, a gamble on the world's coherence and symbolic plenitude that nonsense, glossolalia, and concrete poetry betray by being lexically non-communicative and hence untranslatable.
Treat Steiner's model cautiously, since its reliance on universal grammar is now dated and its male-centric metaphors of erotic possession have been criticized.

Consider experimental and creative strategies for literary and philosophical texts, including Pound's energizing, archaizing, foreignizing style and use of a deliberately non-contemporary idiom to bring out the source's difference at the risk of quaintness, de Campos's transcreation as recreation of the sign in all its corporeality, and Benjamin's transparent word-for-word, interlinear ideal aimed at a pure language, tempered by Ricoeur's rejection of the perfect translation in favour of linguistic hospitality.

Where language deconstructs its own premises, as in philosophical or self-referential texts, apply Lewis's abusive fidelity, an experimental strategy that tampers with target usage to match the source's polyvalencies and bears upon a key operator while resisting domesticating use-values, recognizing that it fails when the source is flattened by typographical changes, dropped suffixes, lost precision, altered order, or unrecreated wordplay, and extend it to abusive subtitling.

Recognize that conventional translation of expository writing privileges the capture of signifieds — giving primacy to message and concept over language texture, so it works by substitution while losing the order of syntax and metonymy that carries the original's textual work — and adopt Lewis's new axiomatics of fidelity, which demands fidelity to far more than semantic substance (the chain of signifiers, syntactic processes, discursive structures, and rhetorical strategies) and shifts the translator's problem from avoiding inevitable failures to compensating for losses and renewing signifying energy; direct any abusive move not at just any element but at a key operator or decisive textual knot — a cluster of textual energy that resists the preponderant values of the usual and useful — since abusive translation foreignizes in two directions at once, forcing the target language from within and directing a critical thrust back at the source so that the original is rendered still more foreign to itself.

When a source wordplay does not function in the target, seek compensation at another point and tie it to the form of the words on the page, provided it serves a central theme rather than being facile, while recognizing that experimental strategies demand a leap of faith from the reader and may be rejected by the publisher as too indigestible for the target audience.

Treat film as multi-channel, multi-code communication (verbal, literary-theatrical, proxemic-kinetic, and cinematic) constrained by an inviolable image that must not be contradicted and a retained source soundtrack, treat interlingual subtitling as a diagonal translation that renders both source-to-target and speech-to-writing, and know the audiovisual types of interlingual and bilingual subtitling, intralingual subtitling for the hard of hearing, dubbing, voice-over, surtitling, and audio description.

Analyse an audiovisual text across its signifying codes (Chaume's ten, only one linguistic, four acoustic and six visual) and through multimodal transcription of frames, shots, and phases with a metafunctional interpretation, remembering that the linguistic code is written to be spoken as if not written and demands an oral register, that its problems are shared with other translation types, that visual and colour codes constrain choices so an unfamiliar symbol may need explanation and coherence with the image must be kept, and that subtitling is an overt, vulnerable translation open to a viewer's scrutiny while the subtitler is often uncredited.

Subtitle within the hard space and time limits of about two lines of 38 Roman or 13 to 15 Chinese or Japanese characters and around six seconds, respecting camera cuts and matching duration to the dialogue rhythm, following the near-universal guidelines to simplify and clean up grammar and lexis, keep interactional features only partly, and render the informationally most relevant items, and handle the recurring issues of marked speech, culture-bound references, songs, and humour using Pedersen's strategies for extralinguistic cultural references (retention, specification, direct translation, generalization, substitution, omission, and official equivalent).

For games and entertainment use game localization that demands creativity such as renaming, neologisms, and non-standard dialects to keep the product entertaining while fitting constraints, where transcreation stresses creative transformation but the skopos is to keep the look and feel of the original while passing as an original.

Situate translation within GILT (globalization, internationalization, localization, and translation), treating localization as the superordinate adaptation of a product to the target locale by substituting cultural symbols and fitting space and as a focal point across development, sales, marketing, legal, and management, and recognizing that in internationalization a constantly-updated interlingua version replaces the source so that equivalence turns on the functionality of the target rather than measuring against a source.

Use translation technology appropriately: CAT tools provide alignment, concordancing, term extraction, and translation memories that speed work and enforce term consistency by imposing existing directional equivalents, while machine translation serves assimilation and increasingly a post-edited first draft; distinguish natural equivalence (naturally occurring terms, as in term bases) from directional equivalence (rendering the source meaning), and weigh the quality, fair-pay, and status ethics of crowdsourced translation.

Use corpora of naturally occurring text to obtain collocation and usage evidence superior to intuition, choosing the corpus type by purpose (monolingual for naturalness and a reference yardstick, comparable bilingual for terminology, parallel for translators' strategies), testing hypothesized features of translated language such as explicitation, standardization, simplification, and target texts being longer than source against non-translated language, combining quantitative and qualitative analysis, and never ignoring the source languages, since source patterning affects the target through interference; distinguish corpus-based from corpus-driven research.

Recognize that subtitling of world cinema carries many borrowings and explicitations and conveys much by image alone, so analysing it needs interdisciplinary film, postcolonial, and translation expertise, and that the visual image remains under-theorized because it is rarely altered and theorists lack film grounding.

Treat translation as more than words on the page, being the product of a process involving human and institutional agents in specific sociocultural, geographical, and historical conditions, and research it through Chesterman's four complementary approaches (textual, cognitive, sociological, and cultural), combining textual and contextual analysis rather than relying on either alone.

Ground a reflective translation commentary in the translation problem exploration space of purpose or skopos, method, and readership to establish the target norms, capturing them in a translation specification that records the source's external features and the target's commissioner-set constraints, since the specification supplies the extralinguistic information without which translation happens in a contextual vacuum where any procedure could be justified.

Let the commissioner's constraints set the macro-level characteristics and overall strategy while the translator decides the micro-level procedures, conditioning translator's notes on genre and skopos (unusual in news, expected in an academic edition, required in a witness statement), allowing a length tolerance for cross-language length differences and layout limits, and grounding explicitation in an assessment of the target reader's subject knowledge and cultural distance.

Recognize that the theorists' strategy orientations align on a single target-oriented versus source-oriented axis (naturalizing versus alienating, dynamic versus formal equivalence, communicative versus semantic, oblique versus direct, instrumental versus documentary, covert versus overt, acceptability versus adequacy, and domestication versus foreignization), and that the choice among them may be shaped by the translator's ideology or ethical stance.

Conduct micro-level analysis with the precise metalanguage of translation (procedure, borrowing, calque, literal translation) drawing on Nord's intratextual factors or register and discourse analysis, and build a register profile of the source (Field as terminology and proper names, Tenor as the writer-reader relationship with modality and reporting verbs, Mode as cohesion and thematic word order) to identify the marked, problematic features that guide target decisions by the target genre's conventions.

Design translation research with clear question types (definition, data, descriptive, and cause-and-effect) and hypothesis types (interpretive, descriptive, explanatory, and predictive), tested empirically against translations, translation processes, or the extralinguistic context.

Design a translation-studies research project by defining a specific, motivated topic, setting scope (an MA works its own data within an existing framework while a PhD makes an original contribution), posing research questions or hypotheses, reviewing the literature to locate the study and identify gaps, choosing a methodology across product-oriented (discourse and corpus), process-oriented (keystroke logging, eye-tracking, think-aloud), participant-oriented (questionnaires and interviews), and context-oriented (case study) research with attention to ethics, and keeping to a realistic, manageable timeline.

Do not privilege a single model of linguistic analysis, but examine a range of models and evaluate each against your own data, remaining aware of their limitations such as systemic-functional analysis struggling with flexible-word-order languages and with implied meaning.
Do not assume the skopos is uniform across a text, since a single text may contain sections that exhibit different aims or sub-skopoi.

Surface a translation's (or a translation theory's) underlying assumptions about language before judging it, because an instrumental concept of language (communication of pre-existing meaning) drives toward information-transfer and typologies of equivalence, while a hermeneutic concept (language as constitutive interpretation) drives toward rendering creative values and social function.

Read any translation through the triad of the translation's relative autonomy, equivalence, and function: the relative autonomy (the features that distinguish it from both the foreign text and native-written texts) is why translation is never transparent communication, and both equivalence and function are variable relations, not single fixed standards.

Judge a translation theory as a complete account of function/goal, operations, and the relation between them (Kelly), and stay alert that the component a theory over-emphasizes tends to harden a merely descriptive typology into a prescriptive norm — so treat such distinctions as historically-situated heuristics, not timeless categories.

Treat most so-called general theories of translation with suspicion: theoretical translation studies aims ultimately at a highly formalized general theory but has so far produced mainly prolegomena, and many purported general theories are in fact partial while being simultaneously too inclusive (covering non-translations) and too exclusive (shutting out recognized translations); the real advances live in partial theories restricted by medium, area, rank, text type, time, or problem — often several at once — and a body of such partial theories must not be mistaken for a true general theory.

Name where a translation sits on the recurrent strategy dichotomies — free vs literal, dynamic vs formal, and domesticating vs foreignizing — and by text type (literary vs pragmatic/technical), and distinguish an interpretive translation (a critical crib directing the reader to foreign features) from original writing that masks its source relation as a new work.

Recognize the foreignizing pole — close, syntax-literal renderings that depart from standard target usage to bring the reader toward the foreign text and expand the translating language — against the domesticating pole that treats any hint of foreignness as a blemish; identify which pole a translation occupies as a primary diagnostic.

Do not treat foreignizing intent as sufficient for an ethical openness to the other: highly literary, nationalist foreignizing projects can conceal an 'aesthetic imperialism' that appropriates the foreign while claiming to register it.

Never let a version's popularity or influence certify its accuracy: a translation's fidelity is always in doubt and varies across versions of the same text, and the equivalence achieved in practice is partial and selective (a chosen subset of the source's values), so the most widely read version can be the least faithful.

Do not assume the received translation is accurate merely because it is the one everyone reads: a flawed version can become the canonical, standard form through copyright lock-in, and every translation is historically indexed and ages as the target language and culture shift, so a version faithful in its own time can later read as dated with no one at fault.

Read a translation in relation to the rival versions it reacts to, not in isolation (translators define themselves against their predecessors, and 'to be different' becomes a rule the precursor imposes); and because each translator distorts the original in a characteristic direction, comparing several independent versions lets a reviewer triangulate the source and expose each translator's investments.

Expect translations to date while originals endure and invite re-translation: a translation issues from a work's 'afterlife' once the work has reached fame, and even the greatest translation is eventually absorbed by the growth and renewal of its own language.

Do not equate sameness of referent with sameness of signification: two words can intend the same object by different modes of intention (Brot/pain) and so are not interchangeable, and the translatability of a work is a property inherent in it, not an obligation that it be translated.

Reject fluency ('reads as if originally written') as the measure of a good translation and reject reproduction of meaning as its aim: word-for-word fidelity cannot reproduce connotation, literalness cannot be justified by meaning-retention, and what truly matters is the untranslatable nucleus — so a translation should incorporate the original's mode of signification (Benjamin's broken-vessel and syntax-literalism), on the understanding that the transfer can never be total.

Follow the foreignizing imperative (Pannwitz, endorsed by Benjamin): the translator's basic error is to preserve the current state of his own language and turn the foreign into idiomatic native usage; instead he should turn his own language toward the foreign, expanding and deepening it through the source.

Expect a work's translatability to rise with the distinction of its language: the more a text is mere information the less fertile it is for translation, whereas a high-level work stays translatable even when its meaning is only fleetingly touched, and a text identical with truth or dogma becomes unconditionally translatable (Benjamin's interlinear ideal uniting literalness and freedom).

Evaluate a translation by comparing it against the source in the source language, giving priority to the elements where error silently distorts or reverses the argument: every negation (a single dropped negative inverts the meaning), every semantically loaded key term, and the function words and qualifiers that carry a claim's scope — and render a difficult passage's difficulty rather than eliding the words that cause it.

Recognize that the translator's chief obstacle is often not the source language's difficulty but the dead, conventional register of his own language, and that there is no single target language but a series of period- and author-specific idioms, so the translator must forge a working idiom and study, not overlook, earlier writers' linguistic inventions.

Never assume that a target-language verse form or genre is the automatic equivalent of a source form: an English sonnet is not metrically the equivalent of an Italian sonnet, so formal and generic equivalence across languages is illusory.

Treat every translation choice as selective preservation: since one cannot keep all of a work's values at once, consciously decide which value to preserve and which to sacrifice rather than pretend to keep all; equivalence may legitimately be pitched at the level of overall verbal weight or effect, and even a deliberately heterogeneous, skewing diction is a strategy to be assessed as such.

Choose the target register by matching proportionate historical distance rather than absolute date (rendering a medieval source in an English whose relation to modern English approximates the source's relation to its modern descendant), while recognizing that archaizing can misrepresent the proportionate feel of antiquity and turn a serious work into an exercise in quaintness.

Distinguish an interpretive (crib) translation, which legitimately guides a reader alongside the original and need not do all the work for him, from a translation that makes a new poem, which falls into the domain of original writing and must be judged by the standards applied to original work.
Recognize that a translation can add material absent from the original and thereby reshape the work's canon, so that later readers take the additions to be part of the work itself.

Check a translation against its own declared principle, because a translator's stated method and actual practice can diverge (Burton professed total literalness yet rendered verse into English verse).

Apply Borges's evaluative method: verify a translation against the source rather than trusting its paratext's fidelity claims or its popularity, detect interpolation and padding by comparing a suspect passage against several independent versions, treat diction that belongs to the translator's own era or culture as a tell of an unfaithful hand, and note that rendering a text's scenes rather than its words crosses from translation into illustration or rewriting.

Value a translation for its creative transformation and not fidelity alone, since the richest versions mobilize the whole prior literature of the target language while a merely accurate, 'frank' version that adds nothing of that tradition can be impoverished; and locate the analysis at the decisive, analyzable levels — the concrete retention or suppression of particularities and above all the movement of the syntax — rather than in the phantasmal extremes of translating 'the spirit' or 'the letter', which matter less than the translator's own literary habits.

Guard against the translator's characteristic betrayal, normalization — flattening the author's deliberate deviations from ordinary usage (which are what constitute his style) into standard expression — and accept that translating is a structurally utopian, essentially impossible task whose impossibility is not a fault to blame on individual translators; correspondingly, technical and scientific texts translate more easily only because their author has already translated himself into a convention-defined terminology nearly the same across languages.

Distrust dictionary equivalence: each language has its own 'internal form' (von Humboldt), so two dictionary equivalents do not refer to exactly the same objects; to translate an author's style, reproduce his deliberate deviation from habitual usage rather than the norm, while accepting that a residual blur (Ortega's flou) is intrinsic because the meaning-shapes of two languages never fully coincide.

Adopt the 'good utopian' stance toward an impossible task: ask how to translate before starting, be first an inexorable realist about the task's impossibility, and treat the perfect translation as unattainable yet approachable to an ever-greater degree by continual refinement — the impossibility admits translation to the highest rank rather than negating it.

Read each language as a different equation of statements and silences whose gaps constrain thought: the core difficulty is to say precisely what a language habitually silences, expressive adequacy falls as content becomes more humanly real (highest for mathematics, lowest for human subjects), and against the dogma that any language can express anything, a missing word can paralyze thought in a given direction.

Treat grammar as an embedded interpretation of reality: languages slice the limitless continuum of reality differently and assign absolute status to merely relative differences, so the translator must discern within a living, anachronistic language which grammatical categories still inform thought and which are fossil forms used only conventionally and ironically.

Apply Schleiermacher's binary and choose to carry the reader to the author: bringing the author into the reader's language yields only imitation or paraphrase ('pseudotranslation'), whereas only forcing the reader out of his linguistic habits into the author's is translation in the proper sense.

Because a translation is only an apparatus that carries the reader toward the work and cannot approximate all of its dimensions (aesthetic, semantic) at once, treat divergent translations of the same text as legitimate and desirable, dividing the work and rendering each facet differently for the dimension one wants to convey precisely.

For scholarly translation, prescribe an 'ugly', unliterary but very clear apparatus that prioritizes substance over beauty with copious footnotes, and render the work's full apparatus — the author's own commentaries, variants, epigraphs, dedications, and canceled material — in appendices and notes rather than the main text alone.

Translate the ancients and distant sources so as to foreground their exotic, distant character and make them intelligible as foreign rather than modernizing or accommodating them to the present, and carry the target language to the extreme of the intelligible so the author's foreign ways of speaking seem to cross into it — since a reading public values that over a version written in the ordinary style of its own language.

Hold the limits of determinacy in view (Quine's radical translation): a basic semantic indeterminacy persists even given a shared environmental stimulus, the parties' conceptual schemes may be incommensurable, and meaning ends up treated as conventional and socially circumscribed rather than a guaranteed stimulus-to-meaning correlation.

Recognize that any de-modernizing or anti-anachronism method can itself smuggle in a new anachronism — Heidegger's corrective archaism-plus-etymology re-inscribes his own outlook — and that every translation, even a strict literal ideal, privileges some particular audience, so name the audience a version actually serves rather than assuming a neutral one.

Flag dynamic cultural-equivalent substitution (Nida's rendering 'desert' as 'abandoned place' for a Maya audience) as a domesticating reduction that collapses the source's difference into a translator-constructed 'shared' referent weighted toward the receiving culture.

Use Jakobson's semiotic frame: meaning is a relation to a potentially endless chain of signs rather than reference to reality, translation is two equivalent messages in two different codes and is an active rewording that transforms rather than merely transmits, and because grammatical categories carry high semantic import in poetry, poetry demands 'creative transposition' into a different sign system.

Locate translation procedures against both language communities' situations and metalinguistic states (Vinay & Darbelnet): equivalence of messages ultimately relies on an identity of situations and meaning is a cultural construction, and the two overarching methods are direct (literal) translation, available where structural or metalinguistic parallelism holds, and oblique translation, needed where differences would upset the target syntax or lexis — comprising seven procedures of increasing complexity.

Treat 'reads smoothly' or 'readable' as a suspect criterion rather than praise: a reviewer who cannot check the original often calls a verse translation readable only because the translator substituted easy platitudes for the text's intricacies, and giving a translation a deliberate 'foreign air' is less dangerous to the essence of culture than a purist vernacular nationalism.

Understand the literalist position and its costs (Nabokov): rendering the 'spirit' rather than the textual sense begins to traduce the author, the clumsiest literal translation can be more useful than the prettiest paraphrase, and the strict literalist accepts splitting the work into form and content and sacrificing form to preserve exact sense — describing the lost form in commentary rather than reproducing it — while still distinguishing true literalism (accuracy of a word's meaning) from false literalism (surface word-matching).

Prepare a verse translation by first mapping both languages' prosodic systems (which differ systematically, so the source verse form cannot be assumed to transfer) and by knowing the foreign literary tradition that shaped the author, then fix deliberate and consistent renderings for his signature recurrent words drawn from the target literature's historical register, add nothing for the sake of rhyme or meter (reorder a strictly limited set of key words but never pad), and where rhyme is untranslatable abandon it for unrhymed lines carrying the absolutely literal sense with the modulations offloaded to footnotes.

Acquire exact information about the source's period, customs, and realia and trace the unacknowledged intertextual borrowings woven into the text, because a major source of translation error is the translator's ignorance of realia — rendering a country-seat as a 'village', or passing off a masked borrowing as the author's own.

Pitch equivalence at the level of the overall impression the message makes, not element-by-element identity: fill the target language's lacunae with corresponding elements so the two messages give the same impression, anchor the judgment in an identity of situations rather than matching words, and remember that dictionaries cannot supply ready-made solutions because word position changes meaning — only the totality of the message determines whether two texts are adequate alternatives.

Know Vinay & Darbelnet's three direct procedures and when each applies: Borrowing (taking a source word directly, chiefly to carry local colour, while guarding against false-friend faux amis), Calque (borrowing an expression form but translating each element literally, lexical or structural), and Literal translation (grammatically and idiomatically correct word-for-word transfer where only the target language's servitudes must be observed, most common between related languages).

Abandon a literal translation for an oblique method whenever the literal version (i) gives another meaning, (ii) has no meaning, (iii) is structurally impossible, (iv) has no correspondence in the target language's metalinguistic experience, or (v) has a correspondence but not in the same register — this five-part test decides the move from direct to oblique translation.
