Know Vinay & Darbelnet's four oblique procedures: Transposition (replacing one word class with another without changing the meaning, chosen when it fits the utterance better or preserves a nuance, the transposed form generally more literary), Modulation (varying the message by a change of point of view when a correct literal version is unidiomatic, the best free modulation yielding the rendering a native calls exactly right), Equivalence (rendering the same situation by wholly different structural and stylistic means, above all idioms and proverbs, drawing on the established repertoire rather than coining new calques), and Adaptation (the extreme limit, creating a new situationally-equivalent situation when the source situation is unknown in the target culture).

Detect a refusal to adapt as a symptom — it disturbs the development of ideas and leaves the over-literal 'sabir atlantique' calque-jargon of bodies that insist on literalness — and recognize that the seven procedures operate at three planes (lexis, syntactic structure, message) and routinely combine within a single sentence, so that command of the oblique methods is what separates genuine translation from mechanical calquing that degrades into gibberish.

Take Quine's radical translation (rendering an untouched language given only unconstrued utterances and their observable circumstances) as the baseline case for reasoning about meaning: it bootstraps from observations conspicuously shared by translator and informant, assent and dissent are recognizable across languages by pre-linguistic behavioural cues, meaning is approximated behaviourally as an occasion sentence's stimulus meaning (its affirmative and negative stimulus classes), and the method must begin with occasion sentences (assented to only afresh) rather than standing sentences.

Hold the inscrutability of reference in view: identical stimulus meaning for 'Gavagai' and 'Rabbit' does not fix whether the term denotes whole rabbits, undetached parts, temporal stages, or a universal, and pointing cannot resolve it — so synonymy is secure at the level of whole sentences (via prompted assent, which crosses cultures) but not at the level of terms, fixing reference requires the native's own identity-and-individuation apparatus (which presupposes an object-positing scheme that may not be universal), and translation therefore imposes the translator's own conceptual pattern.

Treat stimulus meaning as an approximation to meaning only for observation sentences — those with intersubjective stimulus meaning and minimal dependence on hidden collateral information — because for a theory-laden or collateral-dependent sentence the method delivers no wrong result but simply nothing (it fails silently rather than mistranslating); note that intrasubjective synonymy (sameness of stimulus meaning within one speaker) is more robust than the cross-language case, and that a bilingual speaker is the practical bridge, validated by his fluency, by comparison with other bilinguals, and by how well the translations actually work.

Rely on the truth-functional core of logic (negation, conjunction, alternation) as directly translatable across languages by behavioural criteria tested on short component sentences, but not the categoricals (all/some/none), which depend on an object-positing scheme; and apply the principle of charity — an attributed self-contradiction is evidence of mistranslation, not of a 'prelogical' people, so a translator meeting apparent nonsense should suspect his dictionary and build a better one.

Understand that beyond observation sentences and truth functions translation runs on analytical hypotheses — conjectural word- and construction-equations that reproduce the already-secured whole-sentence translations and are then applied, as a grammar and dictionary, even to sentences for which no independent evidence exists (and need not be one-word-to-one-word) — so such translations are corroborated only 'cantilever fashion' as what falls out of the hypotheses: their proceeding 'without mishap' is not evidence of good lexicography because mishap is impossible there, word- and term-equivalences are imposed rather than discovered, and translatability degrades with distance from observation (no one can confidently translate 'Neutrinos lack mass' into a jungle language).

Distrust the illusion of shared subject matter that easy intertranslatability between related languages or cultures creates — such sentences are better seen as variants of a single intracultural verbalism, and only the discontinuity of radical translation genuinely tests meaning — so frame deep language differences as difficulty or indeterminacy of correlation rather than as rival philosophical propositions affirmed in one culture and denied in another.

Have the serious translator steep himself in the source language until he speaks it like a native (an accelerated counterpart of infant learning) and then translate as a bilingual whose two internalized languages play both the linguist's and the informant's roles, rather than by matching words to his own language.

Treat meaning as a semiotic fact, not a thing: there is no signatum without signum, so a word's meaning cannot be inferred from non-linguistic acquaintance with an object without the verbal code (mere pointing cannot teach whether 'cheese' names this specimen, this box, or any food), and the meaning of any sign is its translation into some further, more fully developed sign (Peirce) — meaning is itself a process of interpretation into other signs.

Use Jakobson's three kinds of translation as a working taxonomy: intralingual translation or rewording (interpreting verbal signs by other signs of the same language), interlingual translation or translation proper (by another language), and intersemiotic translation or transmutation (by a nonverbal sign system).

Reject blanket untranslatability: all cognitive experience is conveyable in any language, because where a language is deficient its terminology can be qualified and amplified by loan-words, loan-translations, neologisms, semantic shifts, or circumlocutions (Chukchee renders 'screw' as 'rotating nail'), and no lack of a grammatical device makes the literal translation of conceptual information impossible.

Remember that languages differ essentially in what they must convey, not in what they may convey: obligatory grammatical categories force choices the source can leave open (aspect, gender, number), so a chain of translations can strip a message of content though richer context shrinks the loss; and while language in its cognitive function minimally depends on grammar and always admits recoding, in poetry (and jest, dream, magic) grammatical categories carry high semantic import — gender bears mythological weight — so attend to the cognitive values rather than the words, and accept that poetry admits only creative transposition.

Recognize that 1960s-70s equivalence theory is fundamentally normative — it supplies standards to evaluate translations, not merely tools to describe them — and that equivalence is multi-dimensional: Koller's denotative, connotative, text-normative, and pragmatic kinds, and a family of binary oppositions (Nida's dynamic/formal, Newmark's communicative/semantic, House's covert/overt, all descended from sense-for-sense vs word-for-word) that contrast a pragmatic equivalence so familiar it conceals the translation with a formal equivalence so close it reveals itself as one.

Weigh how far a foreign text depends on its own culture for intelligibility (House): a peculiarly indigenous text requires an overt translation, made noticeable through supplementary information such as expansions, insertions, or annotations.

Reframe shifts (Catford's deviations across linguistic levels) not as the translator wishing to change the work but as functional fidelity — locating suitable equivalents in the milieu of his own time and society (Popovic) — while watching that a translator's minimax strategy (Levy: maximum effect for minimum effort, short of violating a readership's standards) does not, in average or bad work, generalize and clarify a work's style into a dry, uninspiring description; and treat elaborate equivalence typologies as ideal schemes realized mainly for informative texts (documents, manuals, news) and in institutional training.

Treat literary translations as facts of the target system governed by the norms of a polysystem (Even-Zohar, Toury), occupying central or peripheral positions and performing innovative or conservatory functions, and therefore judge not a translation's 'adequacy' to the source — shifts always occur, and even pairing a source text with a translation already applies a target norm — but its 'acceptability' in the receiving culture at its historical moment; this target orientation, with Holmes's pure/applied disciplinary map, is what constituted translation studies as a discipline.

Situate the work within Holmes's constitution of translation studies as an empirical discipline with two Hempelian objectives — to describe the phenomena of translating and translations as they manifest in experience, and to establish general principles that explain and predict them — whose map divides pure translation studies into descriptive translation studies (closest to the empirical phenomena) and theoretical translation studies, alongside applied areas such as translator training.

Locate applied work within Holmes's four areas — translator training, translation aids (specialized lexicographical and terminological tools and translation-matching grammars, since ordinary dictionaries and contrastive grammars fall short of translators' needs), translation policy (advising society on what to translate and on the translator's role), and translation criticism (still often intuitive but improvable through contact with scholarship) — and treat the descriptive, theoretical, and applied branches as dialectically interdependent, since one cannot begin work in any branch without at least an intuitive theoretical hypothesis.

Read a translation through Toury's initial norm — the translator's basic choice between subjecting himself to the source text and its norms (pursuing an adequate translation, close to the source but liable to clash with target conventions) or to the target culture's norms (yielding acceptability at the price of shifts from the source), a priority that is logical and explanatory, not chronological — and treat shifts from the source as a true universal of translation that occur even in the most adequacy-oriented work, where both the obligatory shifts and the more frequent non-obligatory ones are norm-governed rather than idiosyncratic.

Never assume a translated text is representative of the target language or of any overall textual tradition thereof, because translational norms may differ from the norms governing non-translational text production and their identity must not be taken for granted; and take Toury's central thesis that norms determine the type and extent of equivalence a translation manifests, which turns equivalence from an ahistorical, prescriptive concept into a historical one — not a single invariant relation but any relation found to characterize translation under a specified set of circumstances.

Accept that because no two languages are identical in their symbols or arrangements there can be no absolute correspondence and hence no fully exact translation — the total impact may be close but there is no identity in detail — so translation always involves interpretation and remains the most direct form of commentary.

Accept that a good translation faces a contradictory demand and is therefore always already a double interpretation — it must be faithful both to the language and message of the original and to the message-orienting cast of its own language, two mutually exclusive interpretations that consign every translation to a degree of inadequacy — and note that a translator who is also the author of the original can shift at will between conventional translation and compensating commentary, so that for the ordinary translator, deprived of the commentarial option, the central question is whether and how anything can be done to preserve the tenor, texture, and tangents the target language would otherwise override.

Govern translation choices by Nida's three factors — the nature of the message, the purpose(s) of the author and translator, and the type of audience — recognizing that whether content or form takes priority is message-dependent and culturally conditioned (form dominates acrostics, content the Sermon on the Mount), that the translator's purpose grades adaptation from informative through behaviour-suggesting to imperative, and that audiences differ both in decoding ability (children, new literates, average adults, specialists) and in interest.

Understand formal equivalence (F-E) as a source-oriented rendering that focuses on the message in both form and content and constantly compares the receptor message to the source for accuracy: its typifying case is a gloss translation (as literal and meaningful as possible, with numerous footnotes) that lets the reader identify with the source context, and it reproduces grammatical units, consistency of word usage (terminological concordance, always rendering a source term by the same receptor term), and source-context meanings (idioms rendered literally) — supplemented with marginal notes for features such as puns, chiasmus, and acrostics that defy equivalent rendering.

Understand dynamic equivalence (D-E) as the closest natural equivalent to the source-language message, built on the principle of equivalent effect: it makes the relationship between receptor and message substantially the same as that between the original receptors and their message, aiming at complete naturalness and relating the receptor to his own culture without requiring him to grasp the source culture, where 'equivalent' points toward the source message, 'natural' toward the receptor language, and 'closest' binds the two — and which must still clearly reflect the source's meaning and intent rather than be a similar independent message.

Treat differences between cultures as more severe obstacles than differences in language structure, and treat very closely related languages as dangerous rather than easy, because their superficial similarities deceive through false friends (English 'demand' vs French 'demander', English 'ignore' vs Spanish 'ignorar') — close kinship does not guarantee an easy or good translation.

Hold a good translation to the synthesized requirements — it must make sense, convey the spirit and manner of the original, have a natural and easy form of expression, and produce on its readers a response similar to that produced by the original on its readers — which presupposes understanding the source thematically and stylistically, overcoming the two structures' differences, and reconstructing the source's stylistic structures (Prochazka); to translate a poem whole is to compose another poem, faithful to the matter, approximating the form, and having a life of its own.

Note that the dominant naturalness ideal Nida reports — that a real translation should not read like a translation and should avoid 'translator's English' — is the fluency (domesticating) norm later contested by Meschonnic and Venuti, and that when content and form conflict with no happy compromise, correspondence in meaning must take priority over correspondence in style (form being alterable more radically than content while remaining equivalent in effect), yet never applied mechanically, since poetry requires a re-creation, not a reproduction, that blends matter and manner.

Judge translation quality by probabilistic, not deterministic, rules — there is always a variety of valid answers to 'Is this a good translation?' — keep describing what kind of translation a text is separate from evaluating it (strictly formal-equivalence interlinears and concordant versions are valid for certain messages and audiences, not categorically ruled out), and recall that a work's very resistance to translation can mark its quality, since producing a natural translation is hardest precisely where the original most exploits the idiomatic genius of its language.

Test a rendering's naturalness against three areas at once — the receptor language and culture as a whole, the context of the particular message, and the receptor audience — while recognizing that grammatical adaptations are made more readily than lexical ones (grammar is dictated by obligatory target structures whereas lexis offers many alternatives with no rules) and that lexical items fall into three difficulty levels, from ready parallels through culturally-different-but-similar-function terms to cultural specialties, the last of which can rarely shed all foreign associations because no translation across a wide cultural gap eliminates every trace of the foreign setting.

Describe a natural translation more by what it avoids than by what it states: it avoids anomalies (crude vulgarities in dignified discourse, misplaced slang or colloquialism, and the over-precise error of inflating a plain message into legalese) and anachronism (contemporary words that falsify a historical period, or old-fashioned language that reads as unreality), while incorporating the positive stylistic elements that carry the proper emotional tone — the author's point of view including sarcasm and irony, and each participant's class, dialect, and individuality — and fitting the audience by reconstructing how the original audience was competent to respond (Koine aimed at 'the man in the congregation', not the man in the street).

Expect a dynamic-equivalence translation to require formal sacrifices in three areas: special literary forms (substituting rhythmic patterns, e.g. free verse for rhymed or dignified prose for Biblical poetry), semantically exocentric expressions (a literal-meaningless idiom must be made endocentric — 'gird up the loins of your mind' becoming 'get ready in your thinking' — and a metaphor may become a simile), and intraorganismic meanings, the emotive and connotative meanings that depend on the whole cultural context and are the least transferable.

Treat translation equivalence as empirical and probabilistic rather than derivable from formal correspondence: across thousands of cases the French definite article corresponds to English 'the' only about two-thirds of the time and the partitive 'du' most often corresponds to zero rather than 'some', which undermines any attempt to set up fixed formal correspondence between two languages' systems.

Frame translating, with Levy, both teleologically as communication and pragmatically as a decision process — a series of consecutive, game-like moves each imposing a choice among a definable set of alternatives — and recognize it as a game of complete information (chess, not cards) in which each decision predetermines later moves by creating their context; each decision has a fixed anatomy of a situation, a definitional instruction defining the paradigm of possible solutions, and a context-derived selective instruction that narrows that ordered paradigm (ranked by stylistic level and connotation, not a set of equivalents) to a single choice, governed by both objective linguistic material and the subjective structure of the translator's memory and standards.

Watch for the 'surplus decisions' that the target language's obligatory categories force on the translator but the author never made (Russian, lacking a general 'to go', forces a choice among walk, drive, ride, or fly): classify each as necessary or unnecessary and motivated or unmotivated, and treat the necessary-but-unmotivated surplus decision as the greatest danger of misinterpretation, reducible only by seeking motivation in ever broader contexts.

Expect the dispersion of possible translation variants to track the two languages' relative lexical segmentation — the broader the source's segmentation compared to the target's, the greater the divergence of variants — and to depend on genre and on the source's interpretive richness: a prose 'gooseberry' demands exact one-to-one equivalents while a line of verse tolerates near-synonyms and so admits far more renderings, and a semantically broad, richly interpretable source (Shakespeare's complex characters) generates multiple parallel versions where a minutely segmented single-meaning source (Moliere's Harpagon) does not.

Take Reiss's frame: interlingual translation is bilingual mediated communication aiming at a target text functionally equivalent to the source, with the translator as a secondary sender, so some change of message is inevitable (a communicative difference present even in monolingual communication); distinguish unintentional changes (from differing language structures and limits of competence) from intentional ones (made when the translation's aims or readership deliberately differ from the original's), and note that when they do differ the goal shifts from functional equivalence with the source to adequacy of the reverbalization to a new foreign function — which is why a translation typology, not only a text typology, is needed.

Because the author's intention gives a text its communicative function and a text usually has one dominant intention, first determine the text's type and variety to establish that dominant intention before translating, and remember that functional equivalence decays over time and context — a source must be re-translated once the target language has shifted enough that the old version no longer functions (Bible, classics), and a text's own type and function can change historically (Caesar's Commentarii from electioneering pamphlet to informative history, Gulliver's Travels from operative satire to adventure tale).

Use Reiss's core typology, derived from Buhler's three language functions: informative texts (communication of content), expressive texts (artistically organized content), and operative texts (content with persuasive character), identifiable through pre-signals such as titles, medium, and language use (evaluative words and rhetoric signal operative, self-pointing linkage devices signal expressive, their absence signals informative); count a function as a text type only if it shapes whole texts (the phatic and poetic functions do not, since they cross all three), and add a multi-medial hyper-type for texts realized together with another sign system (subtitles, song lyrics, staged drama, picture-plus-text).

Establish the text's variety — the super-individual, recurrent, culture-specific patterns tied to a recurrent communicative situation — and render it with the target language's own conventions rather than naively carrying over the source's (German fairy tales open 'Es war einmal', and death notices and directions-for-use follow language-specific formulas), proceeding top-down through text type, then text variety, then individual style, and fighting the decisive battle at the level of the text individual with a detailed semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic analysis, since form and function are not in a one-to-one relation even within a single language.

Apply Reiss's governing thesis that the text type determines the general method of translating while the text variety demands the target language's structural and stylistic conventions: translate an informative text according to sense and meaning (making implicit content explicit or vice versa to keep content invariant), an expressive text by identification (reproducing the artistic organization, even by shifting to a different figure), and an operative text adaptively (adjusting the persuasive mechanism to the new community, since 'Black is beautiful' cannot be kept for South African buyers) — and because form and function are not one-to-one, render the same source sequence differently according to the type, variety, and function it must serve.

When a text mixes types, let the dominant type's translation mode govern all its elements and resolve conflicts by a type-specific priority — in an informative text retention of content over artistic form, in an expressive text the artistic organization over content, in an operative text the persuasive effect over both (a Firestone ad's 'Foxes use' becoming 'Pros prefer' to keep alliteration and positive association) — and when the translation's function deliberately differs from the original's, drop text typology for a translation typology, deriving the method from 'to what end and for whom is the text translated?' rather than 'for whom was it written?' (as with grammar translations, interlinear versions, and content summaries).

Distinguish the three orientations of descriptive translation studies by focus: product-oriented (describing existing translations, from individual descriptions through comparative analysis of several versions to corpus surveys and a general history of translation), function-oriented (describing a translation's function in the recipient socio-cultural situation — which texts were and were not translated, with what influence — pointing toward a translation sociology), and process-oriented (investigating the 'black box' of the translator's mind, pointing toward a translation psychology).

Recognize the middle two moves of the hermeneutic motion: aggression is incursive and extractive — understanding is an appropriative, invasive act that brings the meaning home captive and leaves the source text materially thinner once its density of otherness is stripped — and incorporation brings the imported meaning and form into an already-crowded native semantic field, ranging from complete domestication to permanent strangeness, where no language imports without risk of being transformed, an immature receiving culture may produce mimicry or expel the foreign, and the translator's own creativity can be submerged by the inhaled foreign voice.

Complete the hermeneutic motion with restitution, its ethical crux: because the translator has taken from the source and added to his own language, throwing the whole system off balance, an authentic translation must mediate into exchange and restored parity — so redefine fidelity not as literalism or a technical device for rendering the vague 'spirit' but as the restoration of the balance of forces that appropriative comprehension disrupted (an act of ethical and economic double-entry in which the books must balance), while remembering that translation is not only inevitable loss but also enhancement, magnifying the original's stature where it equalizes and revealing the source's unrealized potential where it surpasses.

Let the polysystem position govern the reading of translation practice, not just status: when translation is central the translator willingly violates home conventions to build primary models, so the work is more likely to be adequate (close to the source's dominant textual relations), whereas when it is peripheral the translator seeks the best ready-made secondary models, producing a greater discrepancy between the equivalence achieved and the adequacy postulated; and do not fix a priori what counts as a translated work, since a central position extends the category to semi- and quasi-translations — translation has no borders given once and for all but depends on relations within a cultural system.

Study translational norms with their two complicating features in mind — socio-cultural specificity (a norm need not apply across sectors of a society, let alone across cultures, so apparent cross-cultural sameness is coincidence or interference) and basic instability (norms change substantially within a lifetime) — expecting three competing sets to coexist at once (dominant mainstream norms at the centre, dated remnants of previous norms, and avant-garde rudiments at the periphery, so that beginners often behave epigonically by following still-existing but dated norms); model the norms distributionally on a return-potential curve with a tripartite gradient (mandatory basic norms of maximum intensity, favoured-but-not-mandatory secondary tendencies, and merely tolerated behaviour), read a more frequent phenomenon as a stronger norm without automatic upward generalization, and accept that moving beyond group-specific norms to general laws yields inherently probabilistic laws that for now rely on learned intuitions.

Reconstruct norms rather than read them off, because norms are not directly observable — what is available is norm-governed behaviour and most often only its products (even thinking-aloud protocols yield products) — drawing on two sources with their proper weight: textual sources (the translated texts themselves, primary products of norm-regulated behaviour) and extratextual sources (prescriptive theories and statements by translators, editors, and critics, which are mere partial, persuasion-biased by-products never to be accepted at face value but explicated and confronted with the patterns of actual behaviour).
Treat textual products as primary evidence for norms and extratextual formulations as secondary interpretive evidence that must be controlled.

Recognize the relative autonomy of the translated text as the most common assumption of 1980s theory: across semiotic, discourse-analytic, and poststructuralist approaches, translation is treated as an independent form of writing distinct from the foreign text and from texts originally written in the translating language and enacting its own processes of signification — Frawley's 'third code' rejecting equivalence as identity on the ground that 'there is information only in difference' (a translation is a code in its own right, setting its own standards while remaining derivative of source information and target parameters), and Blum-Kulka's explicitation hypothesis holding that translation tends always to increase the semantic relations and cohesion of a text through explicitness, repetition, redundancy, and explanation, a translating-specific discourse type later confirmed by corpus study.

Follow Frawley's argument that a respectable theory of translation must abandon the notions of good, bad, and fidelity just as it abandoned identity and 'preservation of meaning' — since strict fidelity to the source produces awkward rather than interesting texts and would make machines the best translators — and can at most classify a translation as a moderate innovation (a close translation adhering to the matrix or a free translation adhering to the target, both yielding only moderate new information) or a radical innovation that breaks from both codes and carries the most semiotic information, because translation is an act of sign-production, not sign-translation: the new code is a semiotic unit that signifies by its own individuation rather than a universal significance disembodied and reincarnated.

Recognize that detecting a translation shift always depends on an interpretive act: no comparison between a foreign text and its translation is unmediated, because it requires a third term or tertium — usually a standard of accuracy, but also a cultural or ideological code — that fixes a meaning in the source and describes the deviation from it.

Take Holz-Manttari's translatorial action seriously: it recasts the translator as an expert who designs a product specification in consultation with a client and produces a 'message transmitter' to serve a purpose in the receiving culture, so that translation seeks not equivalence with the source but a target text that fulfils the client's needs — foregrounding the translator's professional accountability and a translation ethics.

Hold in view the manipulation and poststructuralist reconception of translation: for the manipulation school translation is never an untroubled communication of a foreign text but a manipulation shaped by patronage, poetics, and ideology, while poststructuralism reconceives language as a site of uncontrollable polysemy and translation as interrogative or deconstructive (Derrida), reducing source meanings while releasing target potentialities that redound unsettlingly on the foreign text, and thereby reviving untranslatability more corrosively than Quine by locating the problem in the inherent indeterminacy of language — in irreducible differences not only between languages and cultures but within them.

Reckon with untranslatability rather than defensively dismiss it — texts whose strategy leaves relations indeterminate through operators of undecidability (as in Derrida) are exceptionally resistant, and because the combinations of use and abuse are elusive and impracticable to program, translation is essayistic in the strong sense, emerging in an experimental order of discovery where success depends on trial, error, and chance as well as on language's paraphrastic capacities — and evaluate an abusive-fidelity translation by three moves applied through close line-by-line and word-by-word comparison: concentrate on the moments of density and intensity where the play of concepts is affected by the disruptive power of language, insist on the transformations the translation makes at the syntactic and discursive levels and not just the semantic, and ask whether the translation articulates its own textual effects that are tellingly abusive with respect to the original.

Distinguish, with Lewis, translating that domesticates or familiarizes a message from translating that tampers with usage to match the polyvalencies and expressive stresses of the original — the latter being an 'abusive' fidelity that both resists the constraints of the translating language and interrogates the structures of the foreign text.

Ground a translation ethics in Berman's 'trial of the foreign': bad translation is ethnocentric and mystifying, performing under the cloak of transmissibility a systematic negation of the foreignness of the foreign work through largely unconscious deforming tendencies, whereas good translation respects the foreign differences through a correspondence that enlarges, amplifies, and enriches the translating language.

Frame translation, with Berman, as the trial of the foreign in a double sense: it establishes a relation between the Self-Same and the Foreign by aiming to open the foreign work to us in its utter foreignness (which classic translations tend to attenuate or cancel), and it is a trial for the Foreign as well, since the work is uprooted from its language-ground in an exile that can reveal its most deeply buried kernel — so that (with Hollderlin) translating means liberating the violence repressed in a work through intensifications that accentuate its strangeness, paradoxically the only way to give the reader genuine access.

Understand that an ethics which would preserve the foreignness of the foreign text can only be practiced in domestic terms — the foreign's differences signalled indirectly by their displacement into a domestic difference introduced at home — which makes such an ethics simultaneously a political agenda that disarranges the target culture's ranking of values to set going defamiliarization, canon reformation, ideological critique, and institutional change; and recognize that there is no true invariant transmitted in translation, since the source message is always interpreted and reinvented according to the target's values and variable across languages and moments, so the very need to 'establish the invariant' shows that translating does something more and other than communicate, and the descriptive turn that studies a translation's acceptability against domestic norms sidesteps the foreign rather than solving it.

Attend to the ideological asymmetries that structure translation: a patriarchal model of authority expressed through gender metaphors recurring since the seventeenth century has underwritten translation's subordinate status (so a feminist attention to gender can recover forgotten translating women and inform translation sensitive to ideologically coded writing), and a postcolonial reflection reveals translation as an agent or subverter of empire, since asymmetrical pressures between the languages of dominant and dominated societies structure the representation of the foreign and can vitiate the ethnographic 'cultural translation' enterprise.

Recognize translation figured as colonization and conquest — a strategy of linguistic incorporation enriching the language of expanding nations (the German Romantics used ubersetzen and verdeutschen interchangeably, and for the Romans translation was a form of conquest), cast repeatedly in imagery of sexual and colonial violence — and that the meaning of 'fidelity' is therefore not stable but flexes with the ideology it serves, defining either the female translation's regulated relation to the male original or the male translator's relation to his female mother tongue, in the latter guise even justifying the pillage of another language, since both versions ultimately certify the translation's originality and enrich the host language.

Ground a feminist practice of translation in the double bind rather than the double standard, replacing the oedipal family model of struggle with a model of collaboration that is at once cooperative and subversive: faced with an ideologically offensive source the resisting translator subverts the text — playing infidelity against infidelity and following out its parodic logic rather than declining to translate it, since refusal would capitulate to the very logic that ascribes all power to the original — and gives voice rather than silence by becoming an independent interpreter who speaks with the work and makes the principles of the practice explicit (so that writing about a translation matters as much as the translation itself), the decisive target being not the sex of the author or translator but the process by which translation complies with gender constructs.

Frame translation, with Vermeer, as a variety of purposeful translational action whose technical aim is the skopos, negotiated with the commissioning client, so that a precise specification of aim and mode is essential before the translator can succeed: the translator is the expert in that action, responsible for the commissioned result and entitled to decide what role the source text plays, since the decisive factor is the skopos — which dethrones the source text into merely a constituent of the commission rather than the governing authority.

Understand why mere trans-coding will not produce a serviceable translatum: the source is bound to the source culture while the translatum is oriented to the target culture, which ultimately defines its adequacy, so the two may diverge considerably in content and goals and adequacy is measured against the skopos rather than source-fidelity; intertextual coherence is the skopos-relative relation that holds to the degree the translator judges the source's form and function adequate for the predetermined skopos (so even an exact structural imitation can be a legitimate skopos), the skopos has three senses corresponding to the parts of an action (process/goal, result/function, mode/intention) and may have sub-skopoi, and assigning a skopos does not narrow a text to one reading — preserving the source's breadth of interpretation is itself a legitimate skopos, since a translation realizes one possible interpretation rather than more or less than the source.

Orient every translation toward a set of addressees even when that set is indeterminate and fuzzy (it may be envisaged as an addressee-type or inferred from the commissioning publisher's range), and recognize that functional constancy between source and target is the exception rather than the rule — the neuralgic point where practice and theory diverge is precisely where texts are lifted out of their environment for comparison, ignoring their process aspect, so that a skopos is always already present in any translation (assimilating or deliberately marked) and the theory requires only that one translate consciously and consistently according to some target-respecting principle: a source text has no single correct or best translation, and every translation is carried out according to an explicit or implicit commission, possibly one the translator sets himself.

Let the skopos, not the source text or the source's text variety, determine the appropriate text variety of the translatum: the same ambiguous will is rendered documentarily with an explanatory note for a court but instrumentally with a similar-effect target ambiguity inside a novel, and a work may even be recast into another genre (Homer's Odyssey as a novel) when a particular skopos demands it — so text variety is a consequence of the skopos and secondary to it.

Do not treat translation as a catalogue of 'howlers' — which leads only to damning all translation or demanding ever 'better' translators — but study constructively how translations actually mediate a work into another culture, accepting misunderstanding as a fact of literature, because a writer's exposure and influence come mainly through refractions: audiences reach an author through an image created from misunderstandings and misconceptions, refracted through a certain spectrum, rather than through direct osmosis of genius.

Treat translation, criticism, editing, and historiography as forms of refraction or rewriting that carry a work from one literary system into another and thereby establish a writer's reputation and, through anthologies and formal education, conservatively determine which works are canonized — an analysis that gives literary translation the seriousness usually reserved for original composition and exposes the Romantic assumptions unable to admit refraction: the ex-nihilo genius, the sacred untouchable text (hence the horror at 'bad' translations), the recoverability of the author's true intentions, and the judging of works on intrinsic merit alone.

Recognize that translation is produced under constraints going far beyond natural language and that these non-linguistic constraints are often more influential than the semantic ones — translators knowingly naturalize the foreign culture (rendering 'cheese on white bread' as 'cheese on pumpernickel', substituting Leipzig for Magdeburg) for reasons unrelated to their knowledge of the source language — so a refraction is a compromise between two systems and the perfect indicator of the dominant constraints in both, the gap between whose constraint-hierarchies explains why certain imported works do not 'take'; how far a translation defers to the source rather than the target depends on the writer's canonical reputation in the source system (a little-known author is translated on the receiving system's terms, a canonized author more on his own poetics), and acceptance depends on the receiving system's need for him at its given evolutionary phase.

Read economic and institutional constraints as shaping which works are refracted and how — copyright cost drives editors to exclude expensive authors, union rules can force songs to be cut, and commercial safety governs anthology contents — and recognize that for the great majority of people, only tangentially exposed to literature, the refraction is the original: a text establishes itself inside a system through critical refractions from learned article to blurb, a foreign work enters through translation combined with introductions and notes, and canonization is achieved and maintained through the educational system, with a direct link between college syllabi and publishers' backlists of classics.

Treat Romantic originality as an illusion: nothing is ever new, the new being a recombination of old, non-canonized, and imported elements rearranged to suit alternative functional views, so a work is made not in a vacuum of unfettered genius but out of the tension between genius and the constraints it accepts or subverts, and treating a text as original requires isolating it from its tradition at the price of losing its history — which is why a descriptive systems approach, unlike committed critical refractions, does not steer the reader's concretization of a text but instead offers the fullest possible set of materials for the reader to accept or reject.

Do not imagine that even a banal message can be translated with a lexicon alone: every message is wrapped in implications and dispositions, so that translating even 'il neige' into 'it's snowing' minimally requires an encyclopedia of culture rather than a dictionary.

Define translation, with Frawley, as recodification — the rendering of coded elements into another code, a secondary semiotic process that presupposes the capacity to code (following Eco, copying is verbatim reproduction, transcribing reduces input into a code, and translating reduces coded input into another code) — which shows translation to be both broader than interlingual transfer (visual, religious, and logical codes can also be translated) and independent of identity or synonymy, since code-crossing plainly occurs whether or not an element of one code is synonymous with its correlate in another.

Model translation with two codes — a matrix code of origin that supplies the information to be recodified and a target code that supplies the parameters for rerendering — and treat the process not as one-way but as a perpetual reflexive shuffling in which the matrix information accommodates the target parameters as much as the parameters accommodate the information.

Remember that the semantic 'essence' of a text is only a small fraction of the total information a source code carries (phonological, morphological, syntactic, and pragmatic information as well), so any interlingual translation that seeks to transfer only the semantics has lost before it has begun; the translation is instead a third code arising from the bilateral consideration of matrix and target codes, which with its dual lineage emerges as a code in its own right, setting its own standards and dictating its own logic — the bane and the breath of life of translation, because there is information only in difference and without the individuated third code the translation would carry no information at all.

Treat the target code as a virtual text — a set of parameters and well-formedness constraints never realized in itself — that binds the source information rather than supplying exact correlated elements, so that literary translation is the mediation between a tangible source text and a virtual target text, and the third code establishes its own semantic necessities that can legitimately override standard lexical fidelity (Tarn rendering 'novia sumergida' as 'bride in her veil of sea' and 'el alto vacio' as 'the rare height' without the text suffering).

When a source text contains irreducible ambiguity — poetic compression or non-recoverable syntactic deletion that leaves several equally plausible deep structures — treat the translator's disambiguating choice as legitimate rather than invalidating, because the source was multiply ambiguous and the target could accommodate any of the readings: it is a matter of performance.

Aim beyond a stilted transfer of meanings to make the text work in the target language with the texture of a piece written for that audience, adapting even the emphasis (foregrounding practical processes and results for an Anglophone readership rather than a theoretical excursus), and ground that aim in contrastive discourse analysis: the systematic French-English differences along modes of enunciation and forms of contextual binding show that English favours actualization, direct constative reference, a tighter network of internal linkages, and consistency of related terms, so English calls for more explicit, precise, concrete, and cohesive determinations than French.

Locate the deep problem of translation not in imprecise lexical correspondence or the absence of a prescriptive theory but in the target language imposing its own discursive relations and its own construction of reality — when English rearticulates a French utterance it builds an English interpretation into it and simply cannot let the original say what it says in French — so treat the difference arising from the dissimilarity of languages as the difference always already in translation, its very ground and raison d'etre, which can be glossed over but never totally suppressed.

Understand that a good translation must sometimes commit abuses (Derrida's Entziehung rendered by retrait) that function not as equivalence but as factors in an economy of translation — a process of gain as well as loss conceived quantitatively — whose controlled disruption unpacks and disseminates meaning, and situate this within Lewis's axiology of two risks: the risk to overcome is weak, servile translation that privileges the 'us-system' (the usual, the useful, common usage) and domesticates the message, while the risk to assume is strong, forceful translation that values experimentation, tampers with usage, and matches the polyvalencies and expressive stresses of the original by producing its own.

Catch the subtractive changes that flatten a carefully constructed source text: paratextual and typographic losses (dropping the italics that set off terms, adding quotation marks the source lacks, inserting unmarked translator's notes), mishandling the source's own foreign and translated words (dropping bracketed Greek or German originals or italicized foreign terms and making do with the target word alone), morphological simplification that strips a term of its systemic value (rendering 'metaphorique' as 'metaphor' rather than 'metaphorics', or 'philosopheme' as 'an element of philosophy'), semantic-neighbour substitution when a more literal alternative exists ('effect' for 'phenomenon', 'valeur' as 'notion', 'articulation' as 'joint'), phrase-level changes that set aside a concept or reverse an argument (converting 'metaphoricite par analogie' to 'analogy producing metaphor', or a single 'condition of impossibility' to 'the conditions which make it in principle impossible'), assimilation to target discourse norms that gives a theoretical text a falsely immediate, practical tenor (added conjunctions and adversatives, a conditional turned assertive, elliptical utterances expanded, an unmotivated participial agent), and the dropping of repetition, parallelism, or a key term's polysemy that carry argumentative structure rather than mere elegance (losing a repeated 'seul... seul... seul', collapsing a polysemous shifter such as 'tour', or suppressing one load-bearing word such as 'history').

Recognize that some texts perform their own thesis — enacting in their rhetoric and syntax the very processes they argue about — so a translation that renders only the message and lets the performative dimension lapse does not merely miss a nuance but saps the strength of the thesis by severing its enactment from its statement.

Expect translation to recuperate a source's disruptive force back under the control of a reigning target-language interpretation (domestication by the natural language), a recuperation a strong translation must run and overcome even though it can never be wholly thwarted, so the practical question is how far the recuperative effects can be controlled and the original's resistance remobilized; and treat weak, entropic translations partly as a time factor, since strong translation derives from an insightful reading gained only over time, and a translation of a difficult monumental text made close to its date of publication is the more likely to be unduly deficient.

Distinguish Foucault's two kinds of translation that map to the non-literary/literary split — one in which something (meaning, aesthetic value) must remain identical and is given passage 'from like to same', and one that hurls one language against another, using the original as a projectile and the translating language as a target to derail it, which literary works demand — and hold the proper aim of the translating act to be ethical, to receive the Foreign as Foreign, an aim that in the literary domain has from time immemorial been skewed into the negation, acclimation, and naturalization of the foreign.

Apply Berman's analytic of translation — the examination of the system of textual deformation operating in every translation, analytic in both the Cartesian sense (a detailed analysis of the deforming forces) and the psychoanalytic sense (the system is largely unconscious, part of the translator's being and desire, so mere awareness does not free him and the practice itself must submit to analysis) — and pair this negative analytic with a positive counterpart of deformation-limiting operations to yield a critique of translations that is neither simply descriptive nor simply normative.

Read the 'shapelessness' and apparent 'bad writing' of great prose (Rabelais, Cervantes, Dostoevsky, the novel a consumer rather than producer of style) not as a flaw but as the richness of its polylingualism, its gathering of a community's many coexisting languages into one work, so that the principal problem of translating the novel is to respect its shapeless polylogic and avoid arbitrary homogenization; and stay alert that because the novel is deemed a lower form its deformations are more accepted and often unperceived — it is easy to see a Hollderlin poem massacred but hard to see what was done to a Kafka or Faulkner, especially when the translation seems 'good', so the deforming system operates in complete tranquillity.

Catch rationalization and clarification: rationalization recomposes syntax beginning with punctuation to fit an idea of discursive order (hostile to the repetition, relative clauses, participles, and long or verbless sentences essential to prose) and pushes the concrete toward the abstract, deforming the work by reversing its basic tendency while seeming to leave form and meaning untouched; clarification, its corollary, imposes the definite where the original moves in the indefinite and shifts the text from polysemy toward monosemy — explicitation being positive when it manifests something genuinely concealed in the original but negative when it renders clear what does not wish to be clear.

Catch expansion and the two poles of stylistic distortion and impoverishment: expansion makes every translation longer than its original, but the added length is empty, adding only to the gross mass while muffling the work's voice and slackening its rhythm (and it can mask impoverishment); ennoblement, the culmination of classic translation, produces 'elegant' sentences that use the source as raw material at its expense, while its opposite of popularization through pseudo-slang is equally deforming — both annihilating the original's authentic orality; qualitative impoverishment replaces terms with ones lacking their sonorous or iconic richness (a word's physical density), effacing the signifying process; and quantitative impoverishment flattens the proliferation of unfixed signifiers (Arlt's semblante, rostro, and cara for one signified) into fewer signifiers, rendering the work's face unrecognizable and making it at once poorer and longer.

Catch the destruction of a work's rhythms, signifying networks, and linguistic patternings: arbitrary revision of punctuation wrecks rhythm (a Faulkner passage's four marks became twenty-two), failing to carry over a subtext of recurring, linked signifiers (or the words an author pointedly avoids) destroys a signifying process whose sense lies in the linkage rather than in individual words, and destroying the systematic sentence types produces the curious result of a translation more homogeneous than the original — possessing more 'style' in the ordinary sense yet actually more incoherent, a patchwork of the translator's different kinds of writing that readers sense is not a 'true' text.

Catch the effacement of vernacular, idiom, and superimposed languages, and prefer literal translation to the Platonic figure: because all great prose is rooted in the vernacular, effacing vernacular networks is a serious injury and the traditional remedy of exoticizing them (italics or rendering a foreign vernacular with a local one) fails, since a vernacular clings to its soil; replacing a source idiom or proverb with a target 'equivalent' is an ethnocentrism, since equivalents do not translate an idiom and to translate is not to search for equivalences; and the central problem of the novel is the effacement of the superimposition of languages (a dialect against a koine, or coexisting languages as in Finnegans Wake), which the heteroglossic novel demands be preserved — so oppose to western translation's Platonic embellishing restitution of meaning (separating spirit from letter and converging on a text clearer and purer than the original) a literal translation attached to the letter of the work, which both restores the work's particular signifying process and transforms the translating language.

Separate Blum-Kulka's two relations: coherence, a covert, potential meaning relationship among a text's parts that the reader makes overt by relating the text to familiar worlds, and cohesion, an overt relationship expressed by language-specific markers — translation, viewed as an act of communication, necessarily entails shifts in both, where cohesion shifts run in two directions (shifts in the level of explicitness, the target becoming more or less textually explicit, and shifts in text meaning, the explicit and implicit meaning potential changing).

Recognize that overt cohesion is tied to a language's grammatical system, so grammatical differences force different cohesive ties that can raise or lower a text's explicitness (French anaphora double-marked for gender is more redundant than English) and languages differ in preferred devices (Hebrew favouring lexical repetition, English pronominalization), and give weight to the explicitation hypothesis: translation, as complex discourse processing, tends to produce a target text more explicit, redundant, and longer than the source regardless of language-system differences — a trend visible in learners, non-professionals, and even professionals — suggesting explicitation is a universal strategy inherent in language mediation.

Treat cohesive ties as doing more than creating continuity — their choice affects a text's texture, style, and meaning, especially in literature — so beware that when the target language's grammar forces an explicitness the source leaves implicit it can destroy a deliberately unfolded ambiguity and alter the pragmatics (Hebrew's obligatory gender-marking and lack of a polysemous 'dark' remove the staged disambiguation of Pinter's Old Times, and added connectives turn a subtle power struggle into an ordinary argument in which neither character gains advantage).

Understand that coherence, as the realization of a text's meaning potential, shifts in two ways under translation — text-focused shifts linked to the translation process and reader-focused shifts linked to the change of audience, the reader-focused ones being the less avoidable — because coherence is reader- and schema-dependent (a text coheres only when the reader can apply relevant world, subject, and genre schemas, so King Lear does not mean the same to a British reader as to a French one); and since a target audience is almost always new to part of the source writer's shared world yet the prevailing modern norm treats a translation as rendering a given text rather than conveying a message to a new audience, reader-focused shifts are largely unavoidable unless the translator is normatively free to transplant the text into another cultural environment.

Beware that over-clarifying a culture-specific detail to help the target reader can destroy the indirect, figurative meaning it carries across a text (Pinter's Hebrew translator spelling out a casserole's ingredients lost the running metaphor that carries the play's marital-triangle subtext), and recognize that translation reverses the residual ambiguity of natural conversation — what is said becoming obvious while what is meant becomes vague; study cohesion shifts validly by separating obligatory choices dictated by the two grammars from optional stylistic ones, since only optional shifts are evidence of a translation trend, and study translation as a process that operates on texts rather than words or sentences (so that its products belong to discourse analysis) and as an act of communication whose processes, products, and effects must be validated empirically, ideally by psycholinguistic comparison of how source-language and target-language readers actually interpret the text.

Make the translator the judge of how much of a source's reference and allusion network to explain — delimiting the central allusions without which the reader could not follow the main argument or plot (Camus's allusion to Heathcliff was footnoted by the German translator but not the English or Hebrew) — while accepting that coherence can hinge on cultural presuppositions and Gricean-maxim violations only a culturally competent reader can decode (Hemingway's 'The Killers' turning on American lunchroom 'dinner' norms), a class of reader-focused loss largely irremediable since cultural institutions cannot easily be glossed in a footnote; and cast the translator in two roles — a preventive-medicine practitioner for reader-based shifts, foreseeing and minimizing damage, and a diagnosing physician for text-based shifts, whose most serious cases arise not from differences between linguistic systems but from the translator failing to realize the function a particular form plays in conveying indirect meaning (choosing a single reading for an intentionally ambiguous speech act, as in rendering Updike's 'I beg your pardon' as a formal apology, closes off the source's interpretive options).

Recognize that the opposition between productive and reproductive work codes originality as paternity and authority — marking writing as original and 'masculine' and translating as derivative and 'feminine' — and that this is only superficially aesthetic, carrying real consequences in publishing, royalties, curriculum, and tenure, since translation is culturally coded as the artificial, false, and treasonous copy set against a natural, truthful, lawful original, a coding institutionalized in copyright law's treatment of translations as 'derivative works'.

Understand that this metaphorics encodes the relation between the value of production and reproduction with power consistently at stake: fidelity regulates paternity and hence property and legitimacy (a translation of non-public-domain work legally requires the author's consent), and translation is so heavily over-regulated precisely because it threatens to erase the production/reproduction boundary by masquerading as an original — a danger figured as the original's death or emasculation — even as translation is materially subordinated despite the academy's heavy reliance on it, with reviews omitting the translator, projects deemed marginal for tenure, and even the best translators poorly paid.

See through the gendered metaphorics of fidelity: the tag 'les belles infideles' encodes a double standard in which only the translation (like the wife) can be guilty of infidelity while the original (like the husband) is by law incapable of it, betraying an anxiety about paternity, so that the translator usurps the author's role to become the 'father' who protects and instructs a text figured as female, and — because language itself is feminized as the 'mother tongue' — fidelity becomes the father's duty to protect the language's purity and produce legitimate rather than 'bastard' offspring, on which logic preserving a text's foreignness by bending the mother tongue to foreign dislocations (Schleiermacher) is condemned as unnatural, impure, and monstrous.

Recognize the recurrent gendered typology of the translator — Gavronsky's pietistic translator (a knight pledging humble, chaste fidelity to the unravished lady in a submissive hierarchy) and cannibalistic translator (an aggressive figure who seizes and feeds upon the original, ridding himself of its creator), both oedipal — and that even the canonical hermeneutic model of Steiner, with its appropriative penetration and a restitution modeled on the exchange of 'words, women, and material goods', is structured by the same gendered logic of possession and violence.

Note that merely reversing the hierarchy — treating writing itself as a 'creative misreading' of a strong precursor (Bloom, Eagleton) — does not remove the gender bias, since the creative mechanism stays coded as male, and that the originality myth is better dissolved by theories of intertextuality that disperse origins into history and codes and by feminist recovery of marginalized women's writing; Derrida recasts translation's impossibility as a function of the law of translation rather than the translation's infidelity, a double bind in which a text both requires and forbids its translation so that translation is at once original and secondary and the difference between an original and its reproduction becomes undecidable — translation being productive writing called forth by the original, which binds the two in an impossible but necessary contract that makes each the debtor of the other and subverts the privilege of the 'original'.

Take the pragmatic, Gricean model of translation (Hatim and Mason, Baker): the translator communicates the foreign text by cooperating with the target reader according to the four maxims — quantity, quality (truthfulness), relevance, and manner (clarity) — conveying the foreign message with its implicatures by exploiting the maxims of the target community, subject to the text's function; but treat Gutt's relevance-theoretic reduction of faithfulness to adequate contextual effects that avoid unnecessary processing effort as reductive, since subsuming translation under ordinary verbal communication elides its specificity, assumes a universal reader craving minimal effort, and thereby privileges clear, natural, easily processed translation.

Analyze whole actual translations across style, genre, discourse, pragmatics, and ideology (Hatim and Mason), transcending the literary/non-literary split, and apply politeness theory (where 'face' is the want to be unimpeded and approved of) to expose losses such as film subtitling systematically shedding, under its temporal and spatial constraints, the politeness phenomena by which characters accommodate each other's face-wants; and use corpus study to seek features distinctive of translation itself — explicitation, normalization, lexical density, and sanitization — while remembering that computerized, globally-governed analysis tends to emphasize norms over innovative strategies and to describe production to the exclusion of reception.

Weight the seriousness of a face-threatening act as a cultural variable set by the social distance and relative power of the speakers (a direct request is less threatening among friends than across a hierarchy, and pronouns of address are a site of complex face-negotiation), remembering that although the underlying strategies of politeness are remarkably uniform across cultures their linguistic realization varies, so politeness can be relayed trans-culturally but requires modification at the level of texture; and recognize that film dialogue is doubly designed — characters address each other within the fiction while the scriptwriter constructs the dialogue for the mass audience as auditors who are often more important than the immediate addressees — so the subtitler must relay both a character's on-screen discourse and the scriptwriter's signal to the audience.

Treat translation as identity-forming and politically inscriptive: it creates representations of foreign texts that answer to the interests of the translating culture and are determined by ethnicity, gender, class, and nation, so strongly ethnocentric translating has underwritten imperialism (rendering Native American kinship into the European identity of property, or inscribing colonial translations with a stereotype that rationalized British domination in India), and although translation can be turned to forge a national cultural identity (Quebecois translators raising their French through world dramatists), a struggle against one linguistic hierarchy can install another, since versions that reduce the foreign's differences cultivate a homogeneous sameness in which doing away with any ambiguity of identity means getting rid of the Other.

Recognize that translating identity-marked discourse such as 'camp' is target-culture-dependent (a French translator omitted the camp of an American gay novel while an American translator amplified it) and that a tool-kit approach, using whatever analytical concept proves useful, shows universalizing linguistic models such as politeness theory's rational, face-protecting 'Model Person' must be revised for specific communities; and take Venuti's argument that prevailing fluent strategies produce an illusion of transparency that lets a translation pass for the original and renders the translator invisible — masking an appropriative, potentially imperialistic domestication that extends the global hegemony of English — which can be countered by a foreignizing, experimentalist translation that registers the foreign text's irreducible differences, though only in domestic terms by deviating from currently dominant target values, so that the ethical choice is between sameness (ethnocentric translating that smooths institutions) and difference (ethnodeviant translating that prizes innovation to stimulate institutional change), an ethics of location whose valuation shifts with the translating culture's position in local, national, and global hierarchies.

Understand that when a culture's referential language is a foreign one felt to be alienating, translation becomes a re-territorializing operation that does not create a new language but supplants the Other's with a native vernacular, elevating a dialect to national and cultural status as an act of reclaiming identity; that marking the target language of a translation ('traduit en quebecois') reverses the usual practice of naming only the source and is thus an ideological act underscoring the language's marginality and constructing a distinct identity; and that translation can be turned to the target's self-legitimation rather than to mediating a foreign work, so that rendering canonical masterpieces into a dialect reverses the roles and gives the foreign work the mission of vouching for the existence of the translating language and its 'people', becoming that community's mirror.

Accept that translation never communicates in an untroubled fashion, because it inscribes the foreign text with a domestic significance: the translator negotiates the source's linguistic and cultural differences by reducing them and supplying another, basically domestic, set of differences drawn from the receiving culture, so the foreign is not so much communicated as inscribed with domestic intelligibilities and interests — a totalizing though never total inscription that begins with the selective, densely motivated choice of a text to translate, continues in the choice of certain domestic discourses over others, and operates in every word before readers even further process it.

Preserve, with Spivak, the rhetoricity of the language of Third World literatures (rhetoric's disruption of logic and grammar), because rendering such works into an immediately accessible 'with-it translatese' strips them of their linguistic, cultural, and geopolitical differences and enacts a neocolonialist construction of the non-Western scene — favouring a literalist 'in-between discourse' that gives a tough sense of the original's terrain, while heeding her warning that political valence is contingent, so what seems resistant in English may be reactionary in the original; and consider Appiah's 'thick translation', which uses annotations and glosses to locate a text in a rich cultural context on the view that a literary translation creates a relationship to the target conventions matching the foreign text's relationship to its own culture — a match that may be unfaithful to literal intentions in order to preserve formal features, and whose value is ultimately settled in pedagogy.

Treat translation as the most intimate act of reading, requiring the translator to surrender to the text — overcoming the schoolroom prize for the most accurate string of synonyms in the closest syntax and resisting both the solemnity of ornate poetic prose and the forced simplicity of 'plain English' — and to construct a model of how the other language stages agency through a three-part structure of rhetoric, logic, and silence (logic jumping from word to word by clear connections while rhetoric works in the silence between and around words), a different effort from treating translation as a matter of synonym, syntax, and local colour, because without a sense of rhetoricity a neo-colonialist construction of the non-Western scene is afoot that no argument for convenience can justify.

Recognize that a translation can amplify a marked discourse rather than merely render it, adding un-source-based material that reframes the whole scene and attributing agency that transforms its meaning (turning a child's role-play into homosexual seduction) under a systematic transformation driven by the target culture's social movement and publisher rather than neutral equivalence — and therefore relate the minutiae of textual analysis to the interactional, social, and political contexts that produce and are acted on by language forms, since translation is about the relation of the one to the other, giving that relationship between setting and discourse the force of causality while avoiding both context-blind text-linguistics and text-thin appeals to power.

Treat the gravest deficiency a target language can pose as not a lexical or morpho-syntactic gap but the absence of a subcode equivalent to the source's — a dialect, sociolect, register, or historical variety — which is why translators struggle over cockney, lunfardo, Gadda's Roman dialect, or Faulkner's Southern English and over whether to archaize or modernize; and recognize (following Gobard) that a community's four language functions — vernacular (local, the mother tongue), vehicular (national or regional), referential (tied to classic traditions), and mythical (the sacred) — can be rearranged by translation, which can elevate a vernacular into the referential language, as Luther's Bible did for German and as translation did for French in replacing Latin.

See a linguistic community as a market of symbolic commodities whose vernacular and referential languages carry use-value and exchange-value governed by power relations, so that a nationalist assertion sets these languages competing and produces a protectionism limiting the circulation of foreign symbolic commodities in publishing, criticism, and awards — and beware that preserving a threatened identity through translation can tip into ethnocentrism, recasting the foreigner as the enemy within so that doing away with any ambiguity of identity means getting rid of the Other and language is made coextensive with territory, since the ideal of a pure, distinct 'native language' is a political postulate founded on an identity fetish and a nostalgia for an Edenic, Cratylean language, an ideology of homogeneity that rejects all dialogism and amounts to a form of totalitarianism, no culture being in fact homogeneous.

Recognize that a colonial writer's or translator's dilemma is sharpened by diglossia rather than bilingualism — the distance between an indigenous spoken language and a foreign written one that share the same heritage — and that populist rhetoric urging writers to 'give the power of speech back to the people' can mask an elite institutional reappropriation, since the writers do not themselves speak that language and the demand really serves to prove a group's absolute difference and secure institutional recognition; apply instead Luther's grassroots principle of observing how ordinary people actually speak (seeking the mother at home, the children in the streets, the common man in the marketplace), because the success of a translation and of any institution built on it depends on a real public recognizing its own speech, and note that a language shared with a rival culture can be deliberately re-defined as 'foreign' to assert its illegitimacy, with the chosen genre staging that difference (theatre's primacy of the oral making the phonetic difference between a referential and a vernacular form audible).

Read the surrounding diglossia as evidence of a translation's ideological rather than mediating function: in a theatre system that has raised the vernacular to literary status the 'naturalist' code becomes the equivalent of the older literary code, so a claimed irreconcilable difference between the two languages is often minimal in the actual text (Tremblay's Uncle Vanya carries the marked sociolect only in one servant's speech), and translators who render the foreign text in the vernacular but explain it in the standard-language preface, stage directions, and commentary thereby introduce an ideology to a public from which they exclude themselves — so that rejecting a long-understood translation as suddenly 'inaccessible', such that the reader must detour through a third language, is ideology masquerading as a comprehension need, in a climate where the translator's nationality becomes a criterion for legitimizing the work.

Detect ideologically driven register-lowering: translators can transpose a source's settings into a lower register and strip indicators of dominant social position (a general's house becoming a village notable's), so the characters undergo a proletarization that makes them speak a lower-class sociolect, and the very choice of which foreign plays to translate can be a function of their characters' social position, since portraying the lower classes reinforces a political message of the people's alienation.

Read graphemization — the eye-dialect spelling of a pronunciation difference ('chu' for 'je suis') — as an ideological in-code of differentiation and exclusion rather than a phonetic transcription, a reading confirmed by its frequent inconsistency (the same word spelled two ways in one character's mouth on one page), which betrays that the 'difference' is being constructed rather than recorded.

Judge whether a sociolect can be translated by the normative system of the target literature, not by any intrinsic deficiency in the target language-system — French can render regional sociolects, so the obstacle is a void in what the French literary institution accepts — and recognize that a marked vernacular (Tremblay's joual) can renew a theatrical aesthetic by modifying the norms that produce the effect of reality and, once institutionalized, broaden which foreign registers become translatable, without necessarily claiming to supplant the standard referential language but remaining one available register among many.
